There is no description of the crate's purpose, how to add it as a dependency, a minimal usage example, or even a link to the struct. Consumers have no navigable entry point in the generated docs.

title: `HttpEmbeddingProvider::new` doc starts with # Errors — no summary line, no parameter docs
description: The `new` constructor (http.rs:22-40) has only a bare `# Errors` section. It is missing: (1) a one-line summary explaining what the constructor does; (2) description of each parameter (`endpoint`, `model`, `api_key`, `expected_dim`, `timeout_secs`) — especially `expected_dim` which is a silent post-call invariant used in every `embed` call; (3) an `Ok(Self)` note describing what the returned value represents.

title: Struct doc claims `direct (embedding)` format is supported but `embed_batch` does not handle it
description: The struct-level doc at http.rs:6-7 states: "Auto-detects response format: OpenAI (`data[].embedding`), Ollama (`embeddings[]`), or direct (`embedding`)." and "Supports both single and batch embedding calls." Together these imply that all three formats work for both single and batch. However, `embed_batch` (http.rs:213-229) only handles `data[]` (OpenAI) and `embeddings[]` (Ollama) — there is no branch for `{ "embedding": [...] }` in the batch path. The claim is accurate for `embed` but overstated for `embed_batch`, which returns `MemoryError::Internal` for the direct format.

location: src/engine/mod.rs:552,580; src/engine/ingest.rs:23,37,139; src/engine/forgetting.rs:23; src/engine/consolidation.rs:16; src/engine/conflict.rs:26; src/engine/graph.rs:43; src/engine/bootstrap.rs:23,63; src/engine/activity.rs:161; src/engine/inspect.rs:124 (Sqlite arm)
title: # Errors omits `MemoryError::ReadOnly` across 13 write-path public methods
description: Every listed method calls `write_conn()` (mod.rs:508-510), which delegates to `pool.try_write()` and returns `MemoryError::ReadOnly` when the engine was opened with `EngineConfig { read_only: true }`. None of these methods' `# Errors` sections document this reachable variant. The private `write_conn()` itself correctly says 'Returns `MemoryError::ReadOnly` if the engine was opened read-only' (mod.rs:507), but that note is not propagated to any caller. For reference, `record_activity`, `checkpoint_session`, `record_outcome`, `delete_lineage`, and `run_dream_cycle` already document `ReadOnly` correctly — use them as the model.
suggested_fix: Add `/// Returns \`MemoryError::ReadOnly\` if the engine is read-only.` to the `# Errors` section of each affected method. For `dump_state`, scope it to the `DumpFormat::Sqlite` arm: `/// Returns \`MemoryError::ReadOnly\` if `DumpFormat::Sqlite` is used on a read-only engine.`

title: `pin_fact` and `unpin_fact` have no `# Errors` section despite multiple reachable error variants
description: `pin_fact` and `unpin_fact` both have single-line doc comments with no `# Errors` section. Each calls `write_conn()?` (→ `MemoryError::ReadOnly`) and then `FactStore::set_pinned()`, which returns `MemoryError::NotFound` when `rows == 0` (fact id not in the table, facts.rs:508-509) and `MemoryError::Database` on SQL failure. All three variants are reachable by a caller passing an invalid id or a read-only engine.

title: `query()` # Errors omits `MemoryError::Reranker`
description: When a reranker is attached and the query has text, `query()` calls `self.reranker.rerank()` (query.rs:51) and then `Self::validate_reranker_output()` (query.rs:52), which returns `MemoryError::Reranker` for four conditions: output length exceeding input, out-of-bounds index, duplicate index, or non-finite score. The current doc says only 'Returns `MemoryError::Database` on query failure.' `Reranker` is a distinct variant in the error enum and is fully reachable when any non-trivial reranker is wired in.

title: `ebbinghaus_decay` is `pub` but documents no precondition on `half_life`
description: `ebbinghaus_decay(age_days, half_life)` is a public, `#[must_use]` function. When called with `half_life = 0.0` and `age_days = 0.0`, Rust IEEE 754 evaluates `-0.0/0.0 = NaN`, so `f64::exp2(NaN) = NaN`. With `half_life = 0.0` and any positive `age_days`, the result is `0.0` (not a panic, but semantically wrong — immediate full forgetting). With a negative `half_life`, the result exceeds 1.0, violating the stated `[0,1]` contract. The doc comment says nothing about these edge cases. The guard (`policy.validate()` in `prune`) is only on the `prune` call path; direct callers of the public function get silent wrong values. Confirmed empirically: `ebbinghaus_decay(0.0, 0.0)` returns `NaN` in Rust.

title: `ForgetPolicy` struct-level doc formula presents un-normalized signals, misrepresenting the actual weighted sum
description:
The `ForgetPolicy` doc comment states the formula as:
`recency × decay + frequency × log(access+1) + degree × log(edges+1) + base × importance`

The actual formula in `compute_importance` (`src/forgetting/policy.rs:55-67`) applies normalization before weighting: each of the frequency and connectivity signals is divided by `ln(101)` and `ln(51)` respectively and clamped to `[0, 1]`. The struct doc omits this normalization, overstating what the raw `frequency_weight` and `graph_degree_weight` multipliers actually multiply. A consumer who reads the struct doc and tries to reason about the effective range of the composite score will get incorrect bounds (e.g., they may think setting `frequency_weight = 0.2` contributes `0.2 × ln(access+1)` unboundedly, when it actually contributes at most `0.2`).

title: dump_sqlite # Errors section omits MemoryError::Conflict
description: The public function `dump_sqlite` documents only `MemoryError::Io` and `MemoryError::Internal` in its `# Errors` section (lines 184-187), but the function also returns `MemoryError::Conflict` when the dump target path resolves (via `canonicalize`) to the live database file (line 201). Callers expecting only the documented variants will be surprised by an unhandled arm.
suggested_fix:
Add to the `# Errors` block:
```rust
/// Returns [`MemoryError::Conflict`] if `path` resolves to the live database file.
```
Insert this line after the `MemoryError::Io` bullet and before `MemoryError::Internal`.

title: restore_snapshot_into # Errors section is substantially incomplete
description: The `# Errors` doc (lines 196-199) lists only `MemoryError::Database` and `MemoryError::Conflict`. However the function delegates to `validate_snapshot` at line 201, which can return `MemoryError::Migration` (future schema version), `MemoryError::UnsupportedEpoch` (epoch mismatch), or `MemoryError::Internal` (zero `embed_dim`, missing root scope). Additionally, the `serde_json::to_string` call at line 328 (serialising `source_fact_ids` for summaries) can return `MemoryError::Serialization`. All four additional variants propagate to callers of `restore_snapshot_into`.

title: get_info() instructions string omits 5 registered tools
description: The MCP server's `InitializeResult` instructions string (lines 66-72) enumerates 18 tools by name, but the actual server registers and dispatches 23 tools. Missing from the instructions: `memory_record_outcome`, `memory_outcome_counts`, `memory_record_activity`, `memory_checkpoint_session`, `memory_load_context`. MCP clients that parse the instructions string to discover capabilities will not know these tools exist. The instructions string is normative for agent consumers.
suggested_fix:
Extend the instructions string to include the five missing tools:
```rust
"Memory engine MCP server. Tools: memory_ingest, memory_add_fact, memory_query, \
 memory_resume_context, memory_list_due, memory_next_due_time, memory_explain_fact, \
 memory_get_fact, memory_statistics, memory_flush_insights, \
 memory_consolidate, memory_forget, memory_dump_state, \
 memory_pin_fact, memory_unpin_fact, \
 memory_replay_events, memory_fact_history, memory_bootstrap_session, \
 memory_record_outcome, memory_outcome_counts, \
 memory_record_activity, memory_checkpoint_session, memory_load_context. \
 Use depth=sparse|standard|full on query tools to control response verbosity."
```

title: EmbeddingSection.dimensions is documented as active but is never read
description: `EmbeddingSection.dimensions` is documented: "Expected embedding dimensions. Used to validate responses." In `main.rs`, `HttpEmbeddingProvider::new` is called with the `embed_dim` resolved from `engine.embed_dim` (TOML) or the DB probe — not from `mcp_config.embedding.dimensions`. The field is deserialized from TOML (and appears in the config example in `docs/reference/mcp-server.md`) but has no effect. Operators who set `[embedding] dimensions = 512` believing it controls validation are silently wrong; the DB-probed or engine-configured dimension overrides it.
suggested_fix: Either (a) remove `EmbeddingSection.dimensions` from the struct and TOML schema and note in the doc that embed_dim is resolved from [engine].embed_dim or the DB probe, or (b) actually use it as the embed_dim source when present. Option (b) is the stated intent of the field. If removing, update `docs/reference/mcp-server.md` config example to drop the `dimensions` key.

title: Module doc claims 3-tier retrieval; implementation has 5 tiers
description: The module-level doc comment says "3-tier context retrieval (identity, core, recent)" but `resume_context` implements five tiers: Pinned, High-importance, Due, Scope-filtered recent, and KB stubs. Every reader scanning the module entry point gets a wrong mental model of the architecture.
suggested_fix:
Change line 1 to:
//! Session bootstrapping: 5-tier context retrieval (pinned, high-importance, due, recent, kb-stubs).

title: Public `resume_context` function has no `# Errors` section
description: The doc-comment on the public `resume_context` function (lines 58-68) describes the five tiers but omits a `# Errors` section. The function propagates `MemoryError::Database` from four FactStore calls: `list_pinned`, `list_by_importance_score`, `list_due`, and `list_by_scopes_recent`. Downstream callers consulting only this doc have no indication the function is fallible or under what conditions it fails.

title: resolve_path silently trims segments — undocumented, diverges from ensure_path
description: The doc comment says only 'Returns `None` if any segment is missing', but the implementation trims each segment (line 47: `segment.trim()`) before matching. This means `resolve_path(" user:michael")` trims to `"user:michael"` and may succeed, while `ScopeStore::ensure_path(" user:michael")` rejects the same input with `MemoryError::Conflict`. A caller who writes a scope path with incidental whitespace will get opposite results from the two APIs with no warning. The trim also means no doc coverage of the empty-segment-returns-None branch.

title: ScopeStore::insert bypasses validate_label — no doc warning
description: `ensure_path` calls `validate_label` on every segment (non-empty, no `/`, no leading/trailing whitespace, ≤256 bytes). The lower-level `insert` method accepts any `label: &str` directly and inserts it into SQLite without validation. The method is `pub` within the crate and used by `engine/mod.rs:532` (inside `ensure_scope_with_conn`). There is no `# Panics`, `# Errors`, or any note in the doc that the constraints enforced by `ensure_path` are not applied here. A future caller using `insert` directly could store malformed labels that then fail to roundtrip through `resolve_path`.

title: `hybrid_search` `# Errors` omits `MemoryError::EmbeddingDimension`
description: The `# Errors` section says only "Returns `MemoryError::Database` on query failure." However, `hybrid_search` calls `vector_strategy.search(...)`, which per the `VectorSearchStrategy` trait doc can return `MemoryError::EmbeddingDimension` if the query dimension mismatches. In `BruteForce`, this error propagates directly from `vector_search`. The documented error set is therefore incomplete for the `Vector` and `Hybrid` search modes.

title: `SearchConfig` doc says "Not wired into the engine yet" — verifiably stale
description: Line 83: "**Not wired into the engine yet** — dispatch requires a second strategy (ANN) to exist." Both conditions are now false: `HnswStrategy` exists in `src/search/ann.rs` and `src/engine/mod.rs` reads `ann_threshold` at lines 282, 343, 346, and 388 to dispatch between `HnswStrategy` and `BruteForce`. This stale statement will mislead readers into thinking the field is inert.

title: next_due_time maps a timestamp parse failure to MemoryError::Migration
description: `next_due_time` contains `map_err(|e| crate::error::MemoryError::Migration(format!("bad t_valid: {e}")))`. A timestamp parse error on the `t_valid` column has nothing to do with schema migration. Callers receiving this error variant will mis-classify it (e.g., emit a migration alarm, apply migration-specific retry logic). The correct variant for an unexpected internal data-integrity failure is `MemoryError::Internal` or `MemoryError::Database`. Additionally, the method's doc comment has no `# Errors` section, so the wrong variant is also invisible in the API docs.
references: CWE-389 (Error Conditions, Return Values, Status Codes)

title: Test setup helpers are inconsistent — no shared in-memory DB factory enforcing all pragmas
description: Each store module defines its own local setup() or equivalent that calls Connection::open_in_memory() directly. Some call open_memory() (which sets WAL mode, FK enforcement, query_only pragma when needed), others call Connection::open_in_memory() + init_schema() without the full pragma set. This inconsistency means FK violations, WAL behavior, and other pragma-dependent correctness properties are not uniformly enforced across tests. There is no shared test_utils module providing a canonical in-memory DB factory.
suggested_fix: Create a src/store/test_utils.rs (or tests/common/mod.rs) exporting a single function pub fn open_test_db() -> Connection that calls open_memory() (or the equivalent with all pragmas) and wraps any error with panic. Use this in all store module test setups. Gate it with #[cfg(test)] or place it in a dev-dependency.

title: Public MemoryError enum lacks #[non_exhaustive]
description: MemoryError is pub and re-exported via `pub use error::*` (lib.rs:52). Without #[non_exhaustive], adding any variant to the enum is a semver-breaking change: downstream match arms that cover all variants will fail to compile. Given that this crate is under active development (Lineage, Archive, and Async variants have already been added incrementally), new variants are a near-certainty.
suggested_fix:
Add `#[non_exhaustive]` directly above `pub enum MemoryError` at error.rs:3:

```rust
#[non_exhaustive]
#[derive(Debug, thiserror::Error)]
pub enum MemoryError {
    ...
}
```

Downstream consumers with exhaustive matches will now need a `_` / catch-all arm, which is the correct contract for a library error type.

title: Consumer traits lack Send + Sync supertrait bounds while async wrappers mandate them
description: Only `Reranker` (traits.rs:124) carries `: Send + Sync`. The other five consumer traits — EmbeddingProvider (l.11), SummaryGenerator (l.43), ConflictArbiter (l.60), PersistenceClassifier (l.93), InsightStream (l.149), DreamCycle (l.167) — do not. This forces every async_engine.rs call-site to repeat `+ Send + Sync` in the concrete bound (async_engine.rs:102, 103, 125, 126, 164, 184, 524, 537), and consumers must annotate all their `Arc<dyn Trait>` usages with the compound bound. The disparity is not intentional (there is no doc comment explaining it) and creates an API surface inconsistency: the trait definition under-constrains while every practical usage over-constrains.

title: `HttpEmbeddingProvider::new()` returns `Result<Self, String>` instead of `Result<Self, MemoryError>`
description: `memory-engine-embed` is a library crate with `thiserror` available transitively via `memory-engine`. The project style mandate (CLAUDE.md) requires library crates to use typed errors (thiserror), not string-typed errors. `Result<Self, String>` forces every caller to convert the error manually (e.g. via `.map_err(|s| MemoryError::Internal(s))`) or to discard the type information entirely. It also prevents callers from pattern-matching on the construction failure. `reqwest::Error` can be wrapped directly into `MemoryError::Internal` inside `new()` to stay in the established error taxonomy.

title: text.to_lowercase() re-allocated inside the per-fact inner loop
description: In `search_archives`, the expression `text.to_lowercase()` is computed inside `for fact in &pak.facts { if let Some(ref text) = query.text { … text.to_lowercase() … } }`. Because `query.text` does not change between facts, this allocates a fresh `String` for every fact across every pak file scanned. For a query over 50 paks × 2 000 facts = 100 000 calls to `to_lowercase` on the same query string.

title: search_archives decompresses all .pak files without using manifest metadata to prune
description: The manifest table stores `fact_id_min`, `fact_id_max`, `t_created_min`, and `t_created_max` per pak, but `search_archives` ignores these fields and unconditionally decompresses and deserializes every pak in the manifest. When a time-bounded query is issued (e.g. facts from a specific date range), all paks outside that range are still fully decompressed — potentially many gigabytes of I/O and CPU for no result.
suggested_fix: Pass the query's temporal constraints into `search_archives` and skip paks whose `t_created_max < query.valid_before` or `t_created_min > query.valid_after`. The `ArchiveManifestEntry` fields are already available in the `entry` loop variable at `src/archive/search.rs:44`.

title: Full Vec<f32> embedding cloned per fact solely to satisfy PersistenceClassifier::should_pin signature
description: Lines 207-228 construct a synthetic `crate::types::Fact` (including `embedding: embedding.clone()`) just to call `c.should_pin(&temp)`. The trait's own documentation (traits.rs:87-92) explicitly states classifiers should only inspect `content`, `fact_type`, `importance`, and `metadata`. The embedding (typically 384-1536 `f32` = 1.5-6 KB) is cloned per fact whenever a classifier is provided, purely to satisfy the `&Fact` parameter type.
suggested_fix: Introduce a lightweight `FactPinCandidate` struct carrying only the fields the trait doc authorises (`content: &str`, `fact_type: FactType`, `importance: f64`, `metadata: &serde_json::Value`) and update `PersistenceClassifier::should_pin` to accept `&FactPinCandidate`. This eliminates the embedding clone and the full `Fact` construction. As a minimal fix without a trait change, pass `&embedding` by reference inside the closure and avoid `.clone()` by restructuring the code to compute `is_pinned` before consuming `embedding`.

title: Active facts loaded twice from SQLite within a single consolidation run
description: `local_dedup` calls `fact_store.list_active(None)` (dedup.rs:34) and then `cluster_fusion` calls `fact_store.list_active(None)` again (cluster.rs:39), both within the same transaction. Each call deserializes every active fact's embedding BLOB from SQLite into a `Vec<f32>`. For a corpus of 50 000 facts with 768-dimension embeddings this is ~147 MB of data processed twice — ~294 MB per consolidation run — before reaching the 50 000-fact safety cap. The two separate queries are intentional in that cluster sees the post-dedup state, but the second load still incurs the full deserialization cost.
suggested_fix: Pass the already-loaded `active_facts: Vec<Fact>` from `local_dedup`'s result (possibly as a separate return element) into `cluster_fusion` so it can filter expired IDs and avoid re-loading. Alternatively, make the orchestrator responsible for loading facts once and passing the slice into each pass. This requires adjusting the function signatures but removes the redundant scan.

title: pattern.to_lowercase() allocates per-pattern per call in hot filter path
description: apply_filter() is called for every tool activity event. Inside it, lines 74 and 81 call pattern.to_lowercase() for every element of ignore_patterns and promote_patterns respectively, allocating a fresh String per pattern per invocation. Patterns are stored in ActivityFilterConfig which is constructed once and reused across many calls. This is O(K) unnecessary heap allocations per activity event where K is the total number of patterns, entirely avoidable by normalizing patterns to lowercase at config construction time.
suggested_fix: Normalize at construction time: in ActivityFilterConfig::default() and any constructor/builder, store patterns pre-lowercased. Then apply_filter uses tool_lower.contains(pattern.as_str()) with no per-call allocation. The tests at activity_filter.rs:154-160 already verify case-insensitive matching and will pass unchanged.

title: Embedding vector cloned twice per fact in add_facts_batch (ann feature)
description: Under the ann feature, add_facts_batch prepares embeddings into a Vec and then clones each embedding at line 258 (into NewFact.embedding) and again at line 279 (into hnsw_pairs). The original in prepared is a third copy. For embed_dim=1536 (common OpenAI size), each embedding is 6 KB; a batch of 100 facts thus allocates ~1.8 MB of redundant copies. Since NewFact.embedding is consumed by store.insert (which copies into SQLite BLOB), the embedding in hnsw_pairs could instead be moved by restructuring the loop to extract it from the NewFact before or after insertion, or by building hnsw_pairs from facts_result which already holds the stored fact data.
suggested_fix: Restructure the ann-gated block to move the embedding into hnsw_pairs from the prepared vector after the NewFact is built, rather than cloning from both prepared and NewFact. Alternatively, defer hnsw_pairs collection until after store.insert() and extract the embedding from the returned Fact.
fallback_tier: ann feature — cannot be fully verified without --all-features compilation

title: compute_importance and graph.degree called twice per unpinned fact
description: In `prune`, unpinned facts are scored once in the filter iterator (lines 103-104) to build `to_expire`, then every fact — including the same unpinned facts — is scored again in the materialization loop (lines 115-116) to call `update_importance_score`. `graph.degree(fact.id)` is therefore invoked twice per unpinned fact in the same call. For a store with N active facts and P pinned, the cost is O(2N - P) calls to `compute_importance` and `graph.degree` instead of O(N).

title: N+1 individual UPDATE statements for importance_score materialization
description: `update_importance_score` (store/facts.rs:564-570) executes one `UPDATE facts SET importance_score = ?1 WHERE id = ?2` per active fact inside the transaction. For a store with 100k facts this issues 100k individual prepared-statement executions. SQLite batches writes within a transaction efficiently, but each call still incurs statement preparation overhead and a B-tree write per row. A single bulk UPDATE via `json_each` would collapse this to one statement regardless of corpus size.
suggested_fix:
Add a `update_importance_scores_bulk(scores: &[(i64, f64)])` method to `FactStore` using `json_each`:
```sql
UPDATE facts
SET importance_score = (
    SELECT value
    FROM json_each(?1)
    WHERE key = CAST(facts.id AS TEXT)
)
WHERE id IN (SELECT key FROM json_each(?1))
```
Or use a temporary table approach for very large datasets. Call this once from `prune` with the full scored vec instead of looping `update_importance_score`.

title: list_active deserializes embedding BLOBs and metadata JSON that prune never uses
description: `prune` calls `fact_store.list_active(None)` which routes through `row_to_fact` (store/facts.rs:815). That function always deserializes the `embedding` BLOB into `Vec<f32>` (line 837, up to 3 072 bytes for a 768-dim embedding) and the `metadata` TEXT into `serde_json::Value` (line 841) for every active fact. `compute_importance` uses none of these fields — it only reads `fact.id`, `fact.fact_type`, `fact.last_accessed`, `fact.access_count`, `fact.importance`, and `fact.is_pinned`. On a store with 100k facts at 768 dimensions, the prune pass allocates ~300 MB of embedding heap data it immediately discards.

title: compute_statistics issues 10+ separate SQL queries that can be collapsed to 3
description: compute_statistics fires 10 separate query_row calls: 5 against facts (lines 23, 24-28, 29-33, 34-38, 40-44), 3 against edges (lines 47, 48-52, 53-57), 2 against scopes (82-86), 1 against events (89), plus 1 prepared GROUP BY statement for summaries. Each facts/edges/scope query is a separate scan. On a 100K+ fact database this is ~5x the scan cost of a single conditional-aggregation query. SQLite supports `SELECT COUNT(*), SUM(t_expired IS NULL), SUM(t_expired IS NOT NULL), SUM(is_pinned=1 AND t_expired IS NULL), SUM(t_expired IS NULL AND t_valid IS NOT NULL AND t_valid<=?1 AND (t_invalid IS NULL OR t_invalid>?1)) FROM facts` returning all five counts in one pass.
suggested_fix: Collapse the 5 facts queries into one conditional-aggregation SELECT returned as a 5-tuple via query_row. Apply the same pattern to the 3 edges queries. Net round-trips drop from 10 to 3 (facts, edges, summaries-grouped) plus the cheap scope/event/PRAGMA reads.

title: list_pinned fetches all pinned facts without a LIMIT; capping happens in Rust
description: At context.rs:79-80 the resume layer calls `fact_store.list_pinned(&[])` which issues a `SELECT … ORDER BY importance_score DESC` with no `LIMIT` clause (facts.rs:377), then `.take(config.pinned_cap)` truncates to 50 in Rust. This means the DB transmits and deserializes every active pinned fact — including their embedding BLOBs — only to discard all but `pinned_cap`. `list_by_importance_score` and `list_by_scopes_recent` (Tiers 2 and 4) both push a `LIMIT` down to SQL; Tier 1 is the odd one out. The gap is visible by comparing context.rs:84-89 (passes cap to SQL) against context.rs:79-80 (no cap passed).

title: Tier-3 (due) fetches all due facts unbounded, deserializes embeddings, then filters and caps in Rust
description: At context.rs:93-98 the resume layer calls `fact_store.list_due(config.now, scope_ids)` — which has no `LIMIT` clause and no exclusion of already-seen IDs (facts.rs:397-427) — then applies `.filter(|f| !seen.contains(&f.id)).take(config.due_cap)` in Rust. Every due fact is fully materialized (`row_to_fact` decodes the embedding BLOB for each row) before any filtering or capping occurs. This is the opposite of the pattern used by Tier 2 (`list_by_importance_score` passes `&seen` and `limit` to SQL, facts.rs:574-617) and Tier 4 (`list_by_scopes_recent` passes `exclude_ids` and `LIMIT` to SQL, facts.rs:677-705). The asymmetry is structurally visible: context.rs:84-89 hands both `cap` and `&seen` to the SQL layer; context.rs:93-98 does neither.
suggested_fix:
Align Tier 3 with Tiers 2 and 4: pass `due_cap` and the current `seen` set into an updated `list_due` API so the SQL layer applies `AND id NOT IN (SELECT value FROM json_each(?)) … LIMIT ?`. Until the store API is extended, a short-circuit at the resume layer avoids the worst case:
```rust
let due: Vec<Fact> = fact_store
    .list_due(config.now, scope_ids)?
    .into_iter()
    .filter(|f| !seen.contains(&f.id))
    .take(config.due_cap)
    .collect();
```
The structural fix is to add `exclude: &HashSet<i64>, limit: usize` parameters to `FactStore::list_due` and push them to SQL, matching `list_by_importance_score`'s pattern.

title: Two `peek_embed_dim` functions with different I/O and semantics share the same name
description: Current state: `db.rs:6` defines `peek_embed_dim(path: &Path)` that reads from a SQLite `config` table via a raw `rusqlite::Connection`. `import.rs:43` defines another `peek_embed_dim(path: &Path)` that reads from a JSON snapshot file via `serde_json`. Both are private to their own module but have the same name and signature — a reader scanning the codebase will conflate them. Neither is accessible to the other without re-exporting, creating a second source of truth for embed_dim discovery. Target state: rename `db.rs` version to `peek_sqlite_embed_dim` and `import.rs` version to `peek_snapshot_embed_dim` (or `peek_json_embed_dim`). Refactoring pattern: Rename Function for Clarity. Motivation: readability, reduced cognitive load when reasoning about two very different I/O paths sharing an identical name. Scope: 2 files, 2 uses each. Prerequisites: none. Risk: minimal — internal private functions.

title: `ingest_from_reader` at 96 LOC mixes line-level parsing, validation, and batch-flush logic
description: Current state: `ingest_from_reader` (batch_ingest.rs:180-276) is 96 lines — the only function in scope exceeding the 60-LOC threshold. It interleaves three concerns: (1) per-line read/parse/validate/push (lines 197-228), (2) batch flush when full (lines 230-244), and (3) tail flush for a partial batch (lines 248-260). The flush logic is copy-pasted (lines 232-243 vs 250-259): same `match engine.add_facts_batch(...) { Ok(ids) => ..., Err(e) => ... }` block duplicated verbatim. Target state: extract a `fn flush_batch(engine, batch, line_no_hint, counters) -> ()` helper that absorbs the flush + counter-update idiom, and optionally a `fn parse_line(line_no, line) -> Option<AddFactRequest>` for the per-line path. The main loop becomes a straightforward iteration over lines, pushing into the batch and calling flush when needed. Refactoring pattern: Extract Method / Replace Duplicated Code with Extraction. Motivation: readability, testability (flush logic becomes unit-testable in isolation), DRY. Scope: 1 file. Prerequisites: the existing `ingest_from_reader` integration tests in the same file provide a regression harness. Risk: low — logic is encapsulated, tests exist.

title: Binary crate uses `pub` where `pub(crate)` is sufficient — over-broad visibility throughout
description: Current state: as a binary crate (`[[bin]]`, not `[lib]`), `memory-engine-cli` has no library consumers. Items marked `pub` are only accessible within the crate, but `pub` implies an external API contract. Affected items: `IngestSummary` and its fields `total_ingested`, `total_skipped`, `failed_batches`, `elapsed_secs` (batch_ingest.rs:146-150); `ingest_from_reader` (batch_ingest.rs:180); `PassthroughEmbedder` and `PassthroughEmbedder::new` (embedding.rs:5,10); `FactTypeArg` (add_fact.rs:13); `OutcomeArg` (record_outcome.rs:11); `OutputFormat`, `truncate_str`, `print_json` (output.rs:5,17,26). Target state: all become `pub(crate)`. The `*Args` structs referenced in `Commands` variants in main.rs also need to remain at least `pub(crate)` (they currently are via `pub struct`). Refactoring pattern: Reduce Visibility / Principle of Least Privilege. Motivation: encapsulation signal, prevents accidental reliance on internal types if crate is ever split, suppresses pedantic clippy `unreachable_pub` lint. Scope: 6 files, ~15 occurrences. Prerequisites: none. Risk: none — purely visibility annotation in a binary.

title: Manual NewFact→Fact field-copy should be a From impl or constructor
description: Current state: a 19-line block inside `resolve_conflict` manually copies every field of `new_fact: &NewFact` into a heap-allocated `crate::types::Fact`, with two hardcoded values (`id: 0` placeholder and `importance_score: 0.5`). The `importance_score` is silently pinned to 0.5 regardless of `new_fact.importance`, so an arbiter inspecting `new_fact.importance_score` sees the wrong value—potentially causing wrong decisions. Target state: add `impl From<&NewFact> for Fact` (or a `Fact::from_new_for_arbiter(nf: &NewFact) -> Fact`) in `types.rs` that seeds `importance_score` from `nf.importance` (the closest approximation before insertion). Then the 19-line block collapses to one line. Refactoring pattern: Extract Constructor / Introduce Conversion Trait. Motivation: readability, misuse-resistance (the arbiter silent-wrong-value bug), and single point of change when `Fact` gains new fields—today any future field added to `Fact` must also be added to this manual block or it silently defaults. Estimated scope: 2 files (`types.rs` for the impl, `temporal.rs` for the call site). Prerequisites: confirm the arbiter contract (only `content`, `fact_type`, `importance`, `metadata` are stable; `id`, `scope_id`, `importance_score`, `access_count` are explicitly unstable per `PersistenceClassifier` doc—that warning is absent from `ConflictArbiter`). Risk: LOW—purely mechanical after the From impl is added; no behavior change if `importance_score` is seeded from `importance` (which is the documented intent). HEAVY: requires human judgement on the `importance_score` seeding choice.

title: Three CrudDecision arms repeat the open-tx / expire / edge-insert / commit / graph-update skeleton
description: Current state: the `Add`, `Update`, and `Delete` match arms (lines 78-172) each independently call `conn.unchecked_transaction()`, perform operations, call `tx.commit()`, then update the in-memory graph. The `Update` and `Delete` arms are structurally nearly identical (both call `expire_and_invalidate` + `edge_store.expire_by_fact`), diverging only in whether a new fact is inserted and which graph update follows. This is a 95-LOC match block where ~40 lines are structural boilerplate. Target state: extract a `fn expire_fact_with_cascade(tx, edge_store, old_fact_id, now) -> Result<()>` for the shared `Update`/`Delete` setup, and optionally a `fn commit_and_update_graph(tx, graph, update_fn)` closure pattern. Refactoring pattern: Extract Method / Template Method. Motivation: the duplication means a future change to cascade semantics (e.g., adding a `t_invalid` set to cascade) must be applied in two places and will diverge in a future PR. Estimated scope: 1 file. Prerequisites: good test coverage (present: 6 tests covering all arms). Risk: LOW—the extracted function is called from at most two places; tests catch regressions. HEAVY: requires human judgement on the right abstraction boundary.

title: 28 identical `spawn_blocking` wrappers with no structural abstraction
description: Current state: async_engine.rs contains 28 methods all following the pattern `let engine = self.inner.clone(); tokio::task::spawn_blocking(move || engine.X(...)).await.map_err(join_err)?`. The only variation is the method name, argument forwarding, and return type. Target state: a `delegate_blocking!` macro or a generic helper `async fn blocking<F, T>(&self, f: F) -> Result<T> where F: FnOnce(&MemoryEngine) -> Result<T> + Send + 'static, T: Send + 'static`. Refactoring pattern: Extract macro / generic helper (DRY). Motivation: maintainability — the repetition means: (1) every new method on `MemoryEngine` requires a manual async wrapper; there is no compile-time mechanism to detect missing wrappers; (2) the boilerplate obscures the logic; (3) a future change to the error handling (e.g. timeout injection, tracing spans) must be applied in 28 places. Estimated scope: async_engine.rs only (28 methods). Prerequisites: ensure the macro/helper can accommodate both owned and reference parameters (see `replay_events` at line 307 which takes a `&ReplayFilter` requiring a `.clone()` before crossing the blocking boundary). Risk: low — the generated code is semantically identical; the macro merely removes duplication.
suggested_fix: Define a private `async fn blocking<F, T>(&self, f: F) -> Result<T> where F: FnOnce(Arc<MemoryEngine>) -> Result<T> + Send + 'static, T: Send + 'static { let engine = self.inner.clone(); tokio::task::spawn_blocking(move || f(engine)).await.map_err(join_err)? }` and rewrite each method body as a single closure invocation.

title: `types.rs` is a 868-line heterogeneous god module with no internal organization beyond comments
description: Current state: types.rs at 868 LOC holds six distinct conceptual groups — (1) event log types (EventType, Event, NewEvent), (2) fact/edge/summary types (Fact, NewFact, Edge, NewEdge, Summary, NewSummary, FactType, ConsolidationLevel), (3) scope types (ScopeNode, ScopeQuery), (4) provenance/lineage types (PromotionProvenance, LineageRecord, NewLineageRecord, LineageSnapshotEntry), (5) cognitive pipeline types (Insight, CycleReport, DreamCycleConfig, PromoteRequest, PromotionResult, FactId, LineageId), (6) activity stream types (ActivityStatus, Activity, NewActivity, RecordActivityRequest, RecordActivityResult, SessionCheckpoint, ProjectContext). These are separated only by `// --- ...` comments. The file is already at 868 LOC and Phase 5 will add more cognitive types. Target state: split into `types/events.rs`, `types/facts.rs`, `types/scope.rs`, `types/provenance.rs`, `types/cognitive.rs`, `types/activity.rs` with a `types/mod.rs` doing flat re-exports so all existing `pub use types::*;` consumers still compile. Refactoring pattern: Module extraction. Motivation: readability and coupling — at 868 LOC the file exceeds the practical navigation threshold; every PR touching activity types must load and scan provenance types; the separation into submodules also enables per-module test isolation. Estimated scope: types.rs → 6 submodule files + mod.rs. Prerequisites: ensure the circular imports (types imports error for DreamCycleConfig::validate) are handled via `crate::error` not intra-module paths. Risk: low — pure file reorganization, no behavior change; glob re-export in mod.rs preserves backward compat.
suggested_fix: Create `src/types/` directory with submodules. In `src/types/mod.rs` use explicit re-exports: `pub use events::*; pub use facts::*; ...` to maintain the existing flat public API.

title: `PromotionProvenance.lineage_id` is a phantom field: `skip_serializing`, reconstructed from DB PK, lies in the type
description: Current state: `PromotionProvenance.lineage_id: i64` at types.rs:217 has `#[serde(skip_serializing, default)]` and the doc comment says it is "reconstructed from the DB row PK on read — not stored in the provenance JSON". The test at types.rs:852 explicitly asserts `back.lineage_id == 0` after a round-trip, confirming the field is always zero on deserialization. This is a lying type: the struct advertises a field that it never reliably carries. Target state: two types — `PromotionProvenanceData` (the serialized envelope, no `lineage_id`) and `PromotionProvenanceRecord` (= `PromotionProvenanceData` + `lineage_id`, constructed only by the store on read). Refactoring pattern: Split into input/output type pair (same pattern as `Fact`/`NewFact`). Motivation: coupling — calling code must remember that `lineage_id == 0` is the sentinel for "not yet persisted", not a real lineage ID; this is an invisible invariant that cannot be enforced by the type system and will eventually produce a bug. Estimated scope: types.rs + engine/cognitive.rs + store (lineage write path). Prerequisites: audit all sites that read `prov.lineage_id` to confirm they all operate post-read. Risk: medium — touches the provenance write path.
suggested_fix: Define `pub struct PromotionProvenance { /* all fields except lineage_id */ }` and `pub struct StoredPromotionProvenance { pub provenance: PromotionProvenance, pub lineage_id: i64 }`. The store returns `StoredPromotionProvenance`; the DreamCycle consumer constructs `PromotionProvenance`.

title: Identical 15-field temporary Fact construction duplicated in add_fact() and add_facts_batch()
description: Current state: `add_fact()` (lines 56-79) and `add_facts_batch()` (lines 176-200) each construct a temporary `Fact` struct with 15 fields — `id: 0`, `content`, `fact_type`, `embedding`, `importance`, `is_pinned: false`, four timestamps, `scope_id`, `source_event_id`, `surfaced_at: None`, `metadata` — solely to call `PersistenceClassifier::should_pin()`. Only field sources differ (`req.content` vs `entry.content`). Target state: extract `fn build_classifier_probe(content, fact_type, importance, ...) -> Fact` or introduce a dedicated `ClassifierInput<'_>` struct that the classifier trait receives instead of a full `Fact`. The trait signature change is the cleaner long-term fix; the helper function is the minimal fix. Refactoring pattern: Extract Method (intermediate) → Parameter Object (ideal). Motivation: coupling — the 15-field duplication means any Fact field addition requires two synchronised updates; also readability. Estimated scope: ingest.rs (primary), traits.rs if classifier signature changes. Prerequisites: test coverage for add_facts_batch path. Risk: low for helper extraction; medium for trait signature change (external trait implementors).

title: `restore_snapshot_into` is a 196-LOC god function; extract per-entity insert helpers
description:
The function `restore_snapshot_into` at line 200 performs eight distinct insertion steps (scopes, events, facts, edges, summaries, lineage, config, autoincrement reset) in a single 196-line body. Each step shares the same shape: prepare a statement, iterate collection, call `stmt.execute`. This makes the function hard to read, test in isolation, or extend safely when new tables are added (e.g., Phase 5 wisdom tables).

Current state: monolithic function with inlined blocks for each table.
Target state: extract `insert_scopes(&tx, &[ScopeNode]) -> Result<()>`, `insert_events(&tx, &[Event]) -> Result<()>`, `insert_facts(&tx, &[Fact]) -> Result<()>`, `insert_edges(&tx, &[Edge]) -> Result<()>`, `insert_summaries(&tx, &[Summary]) -> Result<()>` as private `fn` helpers. `restore_snapshot_into` becomes a 30-line orchestrator.
Refactoring pattern: Extract Method.
Motivation: readability, testability, extension point for future tables (one function to add, not one block to locate in a wall of code).
Estimated scope: 1 file (`src/inspect/restore.rs`), no external interface change.
Prerequisites: existing round-trip tests provide a safety net.
Risk: low — pure mechanical decomposition within the same transaction scope.

title: Duplicated child-index build loop between `load` and `from_snapshot`
description: Current state: `ScopeTree::load` (lines 20–35) and `ScopeTree::from_snapshot` (lines 178–190) both contain an identical 9-line loop that iterates a sequence of `ScopeNode` values, populates `nodes: HashMap<i64, ScopeNode>` and `children: HashMap<i64, Vec<i64>>`, and calls `Self { nodes, children }`. The only difference is one takes `Vec<ScopeNode>` by value, the other takes `&[ScopeNode]`. Target state: extract a `fn build(iter: impl IntoIterator<Item = ScopeNode>) -> Self` private constructor, called by both sites. Pattern: Extract Method / DRY. Motivation: maintainability — any future field added to `ScopeTree` (e.g. a root cache, depth index) must be wired in both places. Scope: 1 file, 2 sites. Prerequisites: none — straightforward mechanical extraction. Risk: low; one-liner callers remain unchanged.

title: build_from_db and from_snapshot share ~80% identical HNSW-init body
description: Both constructors create the same HNSW index with identical parameters (same const `M`, `M0`, seed, ef_construction), run the same sequential-ID assertion loop, and fill the same `index_to_fact` / `fact_to_hnsw` / `tombstones` data structures. Current state: ~55 lines duplicated across two pub(crate) functions; only the embedding source differs (SQL rowset vs snapshot slice). Target state: a private `fn build_hnsw_index<I>(entries: I) -> Result<HnswInner>` where `I: IntoIterator<Item = (i64, Vec<f32>)>`; both callers convert their source to an iterator, then call the shared builder. Refactoring pattern: Extract Method / Template Method. Motivation: coupling (two sites to update for HNSW parameter changes), correctness (divergence already visible — `from_snapshot` has an extra `EmbeddingDimension` check absent from `build_from_db`). Estimated scope: 1 file, ~30 lines reduced. Prerequisites: no external tests depend on implementation details; existing tests cover both paths. Risk: low — pure internal restructuring, no public API change.

location: src/store/facts.rs (14 occurrences of the SELECT column list)
title: Facts SELECT column list repeated 14 times — extract to named constant
description: Current state: the 18-column SELECT list `id, content, content_hash, embedding, fact_type, t_created, t_expired, t_valid, t_invalid, source_event_id, importance, access_count, last_accessed, metadata, scope_id, is_pinned, importance_score, surfaced_at` appears verbatim 14 times across facts.rs (verified). Adding or renaming a column requires 14 edits — one will inevitably be missed. Target state: `const FACTS_COLS: &str = "id, content, ...";` at the top of facts.rs, interpolated in all queries via `format!("SELECT {FACTS_COLS} FROM facts ...")`. Refactoring pattern: Extract Constant. Motivation: maintainability — single point of change for schema evolution. Estimated scope: facts.rs only. Prerequisites: none. Risk: minimal.

location: src/store/facts.rs (json_each at list_pinned/list_by_scopes_importance vs positional placeholders at list_due/next_due_time)
title: Two incompatible IN-list strategies for scope_id filtering in FactStore
description: Current state: `list_pinned` and `list_by_scopes_importance` use `json_each(?N)` with a serialized JSON array for scope IN filtering. `list_due` and `next_due_time` build positional placeholder strings (`?1,?2,...`) with `Vec<Box<dyn rusqlite::types::ToSql>>`. These two patterns are not interchangeable — they have different performance profiles, different parameter binding code, and different maintainability burden. Two different developers will choose different patterns for the next method, widening the divergence. Target state: standardize on one strategy. json_each is preferable: single parameter regardless of list length, no dynamic SQL construction, no placeholder string building. Refactoring pattern: Consolidate Duplicate Conditional Fragments / Replace Conditional with Polymorphism. Motivation: consistency, reduced dynamic SQL construction, lower risk of placeholder-count bugs. Estimated scope: facts.rs, list_due and next_due_time methods. Prerequisites: verify json_each performance is acceptable for typical scope list sizes (expected small, <50). Risk: low — behavior is equivalent.

title: list_active_in_period binds params as [end, start] but signature and SQL semantics say [start, end]
description: Current state: method signature is `(start: DateTime<Utc>, end: DateTime<Utc>, ...)`. SQL conditions are `t_valid < ?1` and `t_invalid > ?2` (lines 730-731), where ?1 should be `end` (upper bound for t_valid) and ?2 should be `start` (lower bound for t_invalid). The params vec at line 767 is `[Box::new(end_str), Box::new(start_str)]` — correctly reversing start/end relative to the parameter names. However this is a silent convention inversion: anyone reading the signature expects `?1=start, ?2=end`. If a future developer corrects the params order to match the parameter names it will silently flip the query. Target state: rename SQL parameters or reorder conditions to match the natural reading: `?1=start_str, ?2=end_str`, then update SQL to `t_valid < ?2` and `t_invalid > ?1`. Alternatively add a named-constant to document the inversion. Refactoring pattern: Rename / Reorder Parameters. Motivation: removes a maintenance trap. Estimated scope: single method in facts.rs. Risk: low if test coverage exists for period boundary logic.

location: src/store/mod.rs:5-16 (all sub-modules), plus all store struct constructors (pub const fn new)
title: All store sub-modules are pub and all store constructors are pub — leaky abstraction
description: Current state: `store` itself is `pub(crate)` in lib.rs (line 44), so external crates cannot reach the sub-modules. However within the crate, all 10 sub-modules are `pub mod` (mod.rs:5-16), and all store struct constructors are `pub const fn new`. This means any code inside the crate can directly construct and use `FactStore`, `EdgeStore`, `EventStore` etc, bypassing whatever invariants `MemoryEngine` enforces (connection lifecycle, WAL mode, embed_dim consistency). Target state: change all store sub-modules to `pub(crate) mod` and all constructors to `pub(crate) const fn new`. Only `ScopeStore` and `UpcasterRegistry` that are intentionally re-exported to users should remain `pub`. Refactoring pattern: Restrict Visibility. Motivation: encapsulation — forces all store access through the engine facade; prevents accidental direct use. Estimated scope: mod.rs + all 10 store files (visibility change only). Risk: low — purely additive restriction within the crate.

title: read_pak trusts deserialized .pak without validating pak_version / engine_schema_version / embed_dim
description: read_pak decompresses and `serde_json::from_reader` into `ArchivePak`, then returns it with no post-deserialization validation. It never checks `pak.pak_version == 1` (the only version build_pak ever writes, engine/archive.rs:177), nor `pak.engine_schema_version` against CURRENT_SCHEMA_VERSION, nor `pak.embed_dim` against the engine's configured embed_dim. A .pak file declaring a future/forged pak_version or a foreign schema version is silently accepted and its facts are surfaced as live search results (search.rs builds SearchResult from them). The per-fact embedding-length comparison at search.rs:78 (`query_emb.len() == fact.embedding.len()`) limits vector poisoning to dim-matching vectors, but does nothing to reject a version/schema-incompatible archive. Under the same DB-tamper / untrusted-restore trust boundary as the path-traversal finding, this means content read back from disk is trusted as if validated.

title: Quadratic-time turn reconstruction amplifies parse DoS into CPU exhaustion
description: reconstruct_turns runs two O(n^2) scans over the attacker-controlled `relevant` entry slice. The UUID-linked pass (filter.rs:102-136) calls `relevant.iter().find(...)` once per user entry (filter.rs:114), and the sequential-fallback pass (filter.rs:141-174) does `relevant[i+1..].iter().take_while(...).find(...)` per user entry (filter.rs:151). For a session of N user entries with no matching assistant replies, both passes scan ~N elements N times -> ~N^2/2 comparisons. Combined with the unbounded entry count (see bootstrap/dos-unbounded-parse-allocation), a few-hundred-MB file of unpaired user entries yields billions of string comparisons, pinning a CPU core for an extended period (algorithmic-complexity DoS). collect_tool_result_entries (filter.rs:217-233) adds a further linear scan per call inside the per-user loop, compounding it.
suggested_fix: Pre-index assistants for O(1) lookup so pairing is O(n). Before the loops, build `let mut by_parent: HashMap<&str, &SessionEntry> = HashMap::new();` mapping `assistant.parent_uuid -> assistant` (and a separate index of tool-result entries keyed by their `parent_uuid`). Replace the inner `.find()` at filter.rs:114 with `by_parent.get(user_uuid.as_str())`, and replace the linear scan in collect_tool_result_entries with a lookup into the tool-result index. This reduces total work to O(n). Independently, capping MAX_ENTRIES (per the parse fix) bounds the worst case even if the algorithm is left quadratic.

title: Unbounded full-document JSON parse of attacker-controlled snapshot to read one field
description: `peek_embed_dim` wraps the snapshot file in a `BufReader` and calls `serde_json::from_reader::<SnapshotHeader>(reader)` to extract a single `embed_dim: usize`. serde_json does not stop after the known field — it tokenizes and validates the ENTIRE JSON document up to EOF, allocating intermediate `String`/buffer storage for arbitrarily large object keys and values. There is no `.take(N)` byte cap on the reader. The snapshot file is the import source, i.e. fully attacker-controlled input (the trust boundary). This runs only on the plain-JSON path (when `--embed-dim` is omitted), but in that case a multi-GB or pathological header drives unbounded memory allocation before `restore_json` (which the inspect-module audit notes has its own 4 GiB cap) is ever reached. This is a redundant, uncapped pre-parse introduced by the CLI itself, separate from the engine's restore path. serde_json's default 128-deep recursion limit bounds the nesting/stack-overflow vector but NOT total width/bytes. CWE-400, CWE-770.

title: No per-line length cap on JSONL ingest — single unterminated line forces unbounded allocation
description: `ingest_from_reader` iterates `BufReader::lines()` over the JSONL input (file or stdin), which the `--file` argument makes attacker-controllable (the trust boundary). `lines()` allocates one heap `String` per line with NO length cap: a single multi-GB line containing no `\n` forces the reader to buffer the entire blob into one `String` before `serde_json::from_str` even runs. The `batch_size` parameter bounds the in-flight `Vec<AddFactRequest>` (flushed every `batch_size` lines), but does nothing to bound an individual line's size. This is the same class flagged in the bootstrap-module parse loop, re-introduced at the CLI boundary. CWE-400, CWE-770, CWE-789.

title: SQLite write transaction held open across consumer LLM/network calls (DoS / lock starvation)
description: consolidate() opens a single write transaction at mod.rs:50 (conn.unchecked_transaction()) and keeps it open for the entire 3-pass pipeline. Inside that transaction, cluster_fusion calls generator.summarize(&cluster_facts)? and generator.embed(&summary_text)? (cluster.rs:70-71), and global_integration does the same (global.rs:59-60). Per the crate's own design contract, SummaryGenerator delegates ALL LLM/network work to the consumer, so these are unbounded-latency network round-trips. The SQLite write lock is held for the full duration. The engine wraps its write connection in a Mutex (verified: src/engine/mod.rs:508 `fn write_conn(&self) -> Result<MutexGuard<'_, Connection>>`), so a slow, timing-out, or hanging consumer endpoint serializes and stalls the entire engine's write path — every concurrent writer blocks for the round-trip duration. WAL mode keeps readers alive but does not help writers. A consumer with N clusters makes N sequential blocking network calls under the lock. This is the only finding in scope with a real availability attack surface.
suggested_fix: Do not hold the write transaction across consumer trait calls. Restructure each pass to: (1) read fact/summary inputs under a short read scope, (2) drop the lock and invoke generator.summarize/embed with no transaction held, (3) re-acquire and open a short write transaction only to insert the produced summaries. Example for cluster_fusion: collect all (cluster_facts, source_ids, scope_id) first, release the tx, run all summarize/embed calls, then open a fresh tx for the batch of summary_store.insert(...) calls. Optionally document a consumer-side timeout requirement on SummaryGenerator. Note this trades the current single-transaction atomicity for per-batch atomicity — acceptable since consolidation is idempotent (delete_by_level + rebuild).

title: Byte-index slice on UTF-8 response body panics on multi-byte codepoint (reachable DoS)
description: In embed_batch, when the response is in an unrecognized format, the code builds an error message by truncating the re-serialized body: `let truncated = if body_str.len() > 1000 { format!("{}... (truncated)", &body_str[..1000]) } ...`. `body_str` comes from `serde_json::to_string(&body)`, and serde_json's default CompactFormatter emits raw (non-`\u`-escaped) multi-byte UTF-8 for non-ASCII content. `&body_str[..1000]` is a BYTE index, so if byte 1000 falls inside a multi-byte codepoint (trivially the case for any response containing CJK text, accented characters, or emoji in an error/model field), the slice panics: 'byte index 1000 is not a char boundary'. I empirically confirmed both that such a slice panics (a 3-byte 'あ' straddling index 1000) and that serde_json does not escape non-ASCII by default. The endpoint is consumer-configured but a misbehaving/misconfigured/compromised endpoint can return such a body, turning a parse-failure path into a process panic (denial of service). The crate forbids unsafe, so this is a safe panic, not memory corruption.

title: Unbounded HTTP response body read into memory (no size cap) — resource-exhaustion DoS
description: Both embed() and embed_batch() consume the full HTTP response with `resp.json()` (lines 138, 209) and, on the error path, `resp.text()` (lines 132, 203). reqwest::blocking::Response::json()/text() buffer the entire body into memory with no length limit. A compromised, buggy, or misconfigured endpoint (e.g. a URL accidentally pointed at a large HTML page or an adversarial server streaming gigabytes) causes unbounded allocation and can OOM the host agent. There is a timeout on the client (good) but no body-size cap, and a slow-trickle large body can stay under the timeout while exhausting memory. This is the only crate in the workspace with a live network dependency, so this is the primary inbound-network resource-exhaustion vector.

title: Unbounded MessagePack deserialization of .snapshot sidecar (allocation DoS)
description:
`load_from_file()` reads the entire `.snapshot` sidecar into memory with `fs::read(path)` (line 210, no size cap) and then deserializes the payload with `rmp_serde::from_slice` (line 277) into `SnapshotPayload`, which contains `Vec<GraphEdgeSnapshot>`, `Vec<ScopeNode>`, and `Vec<HnswEntry>` (each `HnswEntry` holding a `Vec<f32>` embedding). rmp-serde 1.3.1 honors the MessagePack array-length prefix via serde's `size_hint`, so the derived `Visitor` performs `Vec::with_capacity(declared_len)` BEFORE consuming elements. A crafted file that declares a huge array length forces a large up-front allocation (memory-exhaustion / OOM-abort DoS) even though the file itself is small.

The blake3 checksum (verified at line 270, before payload deserialize at 277) is the only gate, but blake3 here is UNKEYED and serves as a corruption/integrity check, not an authentication control: any actor able to write the sidecar can recompute a matching blake3 over a malicious payload. The header is deserialized at line 241 BEFORE the checksum check, but `SnapshotHeader` holds only scalar fields, so the amplification risk is confined to the payload path.

Threat model: exploitation requires write access to the `<db>.snapshot` file in the engine's own data directory, so this is a local tamper / shared-data-dir DoS rather than a remote one — hence medium, not high. The flat (non-recursive) snapshot types mean there is no stack-overflow/recursion-depth angle here; the concern is purely unbounded allocation. CWE-502, CWE-400, CWE-789.

title: Unbounded edge allocation in MemoryGraph::from_snapshot from deserialized snapshot Vec
description: MemoryGraph::from_snapshot iterates snap.edges (a Vec<GraphEdgeSnapshot> with no length cap, deserialized from the .snapshot sidecar via rmp_serde in engine/snapshot.rs:277) and calls add_edge for each, allocating petgraph nodes and edges plus HashMap entries. There is no bound on the number of edges processed. The snapshot is a local-filesystem sidecar that is (a) integrity-checked with blake3 (engine/snapshot.rs:270) and (b) gated by a DB fingerprint that requires active_edge_count/max_edge_id to match the live DB (engine/snapshot.rs:333). Note blake3 here is an unkeyed hash: it defends against accidental corruption, not against a local actor who can replace the sidecar (such an actor also controls the adjacent DB file). The fingerprint constraint meaningfully bounds the allocation to roughly the real graph size, which is why this is medium and not high. Residual risk: an attacker who can also rewrite the DB to inflate the edge count (so the fingerprint still matches an oversized snapshot) can drive large allocation at cold-start (CWE-400/770), and the raw rmp_serde::from_slice of payload_bytes has no element-count limit (CWE-502 unbounded-collection DoS). Severity would rise to high if snapshots ever became network- or multi-tenant-sourced.

title: Restore trusts per-fact/per-summary embedding dimension without validating against embed_dim
description: restore_snapshot_into validates only the top-level snapshot.embed_dim (validate_snapshot checks it is non-zero; engine/restore.rs:31 matches it to config.embed_dim). It never validates that each fact.embedding / summary.embedding has length == snapshot.embed_dim. restore.rs:264 calls serialize_embedding(&fact.embedding) and restore.rs:326 serialize_embedding(&summary.embedding) on attacker-controlled vectors of arbitrary length (including empty), writing mismatched BLOBs into the DB. These rows then fail at read time: deserialize_embedding (src/store/mod.rs:47) returns EmbeddingDimension when blob.len() != dim*4, so a single crafted fact poisons subsequent reads / vector-index loads of that row. This is the same blind-trust-of-deserialized-blob class flagged for the engine HNSW path, except HNSW entries ARE dim-validated on load and facts/summaries here are NOT. CWE-20 (improper input validation), CWE-1284 (improper validation of quantity in input).

title: memory_dump_state path guard follows symlinks on leaf and has a check-to-use (TOCTOU) window
description: The guard canonicalizes the PARENT directory and checks canonical.starts_with(temp_dir()). Canonicalizing the parent correctly defeats '..' traversal (this is stronger than a lexical starts_with check). However: (1) the leaf filename component is never canonicalized, so if an attacker who can write to the temp dir places a symlink there (e.g. /tmp/x -> /home/user/.ssh/authorized_keys), the downstream File::create / fs::rename in src/inspect/dump.rs:115,119 follows it and writes engine-snapshot JSON outside the temp jail (CWE-59). (2) There is a TOCTOU gap between std::fs::canonicalize(parent) here and the later File::create/rename in dump.rs — the parent (or a path component) can be swapped after the check (CWE-367). Practical severity is bounded by the precondition of prior write access to the temp directory, and the written content is a memory snapshot rather than fully attacker-chosen bytes. Note: std::env::temp_dir() also honors TMPDIR/TMP/TEMP, but those are operator launch-time env, not client-controllable over JSON-RPC, so they are not part of this finding.
suggested_fix: Resolve and reject symlinks on the full target and create atomically. Canonicalize the leaf if it exists and re-check containment; create the dump via tempfile::NamedTempFile in the temp dir then persist, or open the destination with OpenOptions::new().write(true).create_new(true).custom_flags(libc::O_NOFOLLOW) so an existing symlink leaf fails. Simplest robust fix: ignore the client-supplied directory entirely and always write to a freshly minted tempfile::Builder path inside std::env::temp_dir(), returning the generated path — the client does not need to choose the location.

title: Unbounded read_pool_size leads to FD exhaustion / large allocation (CWE-770/789)
description: `ConnectionPool::open` and `open_read_only` take `read_pool_size: usize` directly from the consumer-facing `EngineConfig.read_pool_size` (a `pub usize` field in src/engine/mod.rs:63 with no upper-bound validation). It flows unchecked into `Vec::with_capacity(read_pool_size)` (line 98 / 166) and a `for _ in 0..read_pool_size` loop that opens that many SQLite connections (lines 99-104 / 167-170). A large value (e.g. millions, or usize::MAX) attempts an oversized capacity reservation and/or exhausts the process file-descriptor table, each open being a real OS handle. This is consumer-controlled rather than network-attacker-controlled (embedded in-process library), which bounds the severity, but there is no defensive cap and no error returned before resource pressure. CWE-770 (Allocation of Resources Without Limits), CWE-789 (Memory Allocation with Excessive Size Value).
suggested_fix: Clamp at the pool boundary so the invariant is enforced regardless of caller: `const MAX_READ_POOL: usize = 256; let read_pool_size = read_pool_size.min(MAX_READ_POOL);` before `Vec::with_capacity(...)`. Alternatively return `MemoryError` for values above the cap so the misconfiguration is surfaced rather than silently clamped. Apply identically in `open` and `open_read_only`.

title: Unbounded parent-chain / BFS traversal over unvalidated tree structure (snapshot-injected parent_id cycle -> infinite loop DoS)
description: ScopeTree traversal assumes the node graph is an acyclic tree but never enforces it. ancestors() (tree.rs:61), inherited() (tree.rs:91), and path_for_id() (tree.rs:147) walk the parent_id chain with `while let Some(id) = current { ...; current = node.parent_id }` and no visited-set or depth bound. subtree() (tree.rs:72) does a BFS over the children map with no visited set. The children map and node set are built from ScopeNode data WITHOUT any tree-integrity validation in both build paths: from_snapshot() (tree.rs:178) and insert() (tree.rs:117). ScopeNode derives Serialize+Deserialize (types.rs:172) and the snapshot payload carries `ScopeTreeSnapshot { nodes: Vec<ScopeNode> }` (engine/snapshot.rs:91), deserialized from the on-disk `.snapshot` sidecar via rmp_serde::from_slice in load_from_file (engine/snapshot.rs:277). The engine memory for this codebase classifies snapshot deserialize as the live untrusted-input vector, so this is not theoretical. The blake3 checksum in load_from_file (engine/snapshot.rs:270) is an integrity check computed over the attacker-supplied bytes, not authentication, and the fingerprint comparison in engine/mod.rs:333 only checks max_scope_id/scope_count, never parent-chain integrity. An attacker (or DB/file corruption) that writes a snapshot whose nodes contain a parent_id cycle (e.g. A.parent_id=B, B.parent_id=A) causes from_snapshot to build children[A]=[B], children[B]=[A]; the very next call to any traversal hangs the calling thread forever. Reachable from: engine/query.rs:26/94 (resolve_query), engine/resume.rs:32 and engine/mod.rs:668 (ancestors), engine/graph.rs:51 and engine/activity.rs:211 (subtree), inspect/explain.rs:73 (path_for_id). A self-parenting or cyclic node also makes inherited()/subtree() grow `result` without bound (memory exhaustion) before the loop is even noticed. CWE-835 is the primary defect (loop with unreachable exit condition over attacker-influenced graph); CWE-400 is the consequence. This is one root cause across all five sites, not five findings.

title: pub write() bypasses the read-only guard enforced by try_write()
description: ConnectionPool::write() (line 206) locks and returns the write connection unconditionally with no check on self.read_only. ConnectionPool::try_write() (line 213-218) is the only method that enforces the ReadOnly invariant. Because write() is pub, any caller that reaches the pool directly — rather than through the engine's write_conn() helper — can acquire a mutable connection on a database that was opened with SQLITE_OPEN_READ_ONLY flags, causing an SQLite error at execution time instead of a clean MemoryError::ReadOnly. Today engine/restore.rs lines 55 and 84 call pool.write() directly without checking is_read_only() first. If restore paths ever become reachable on a read-only engine the SQLite-level error will surface rather than the typed error.
_verified: VERIFIED: query_only=ON backstops write_conn in RO pool + callers use writable pools — defense-in-depth footgun, not live vuln

title: Post-commit graph mutation creates a split-brain window if a panic occurs between DB commit and graph update
description: In all three mutation branches, `tx.commit()?` succeeds first, then the in-memory `MemoryGraph` is mutated (e.g. `graph.add_edge(...)`, `graph.remove_edges_by_fact(...)`). A panic between the commit and the graph mutation leaves the DB and graph diverged for the rest of the session. The engine recovers on the next `open()` via `MemoryGraph::load_from_db`, but within-session query results (graph neighbors, degree-based importance scoring) will be wrong. This is a safe-Rust soundness concern: no invariant in the type system prevents the partial state.
suggested_fix: Document the invariant explicitly in the function doc and in `MemoryGraph` that the graph is eventually consistent, recovered on `open()`. Longer-term: consider a two-phase approach where the graph is updated speculatively before commit and rolled back on `tx.commit()` failure, trading the split-brain from the post-commit panic window (rare) for a pre-commit rollback (reliable). Alternatively, validate with `debug_assert!(graph_and_db_consistent())` in tests to catch drift early.

title: Debug-derived strings used for on-disk SQL serialization of FactType and ConsolidationLevel
description: restore_snapshot_into serializes fact_type and summary level via format!("{:?}", ...).to_lowercase() (lines 265 and 327). FactType and ConsolidationLevel already implement Display with the exact lowercase strings the DB schema expects (src/types.rs:59-67, 77-85). Using Debug output for an on-disk schema is fragile: if a variant is renamed or PascalCase changes (e.g. WorkingMemory -> 'workingmemory' not 'working_memory'), the persisted snapshot diverges silently from what FactStore reads via the canonical Display/parse path. The module is internally inconsistent: events use the dedicated event_type_to_str() helper (line 236) while facts and summaries take the Debug shortcut.
suggested_fix: Line 265: `let ft = fact.fact_type.to_string();`  Line 327: `let level = summary.level.to_string();`  Output is byte-identical with the existing Display impls; this removes the implicit dependency on Debug-derive stability.

title: 226 clippy warnings backlog
no cargo-audit/deny/deny.toml advisory gate
ArchivePak serde roundtrip uses vec![] for facts and edges — bi-temporal fields, embeddings, and is_pinned never exercised
description: The test archive_pak_roundtrip_serde (types.rs:86) constructs an ArchivePak with facts: vec![] and edges: vec![] (lines 92-93). It asserts only on pak_version and embed_dim after deserialization — it does not verify that facts or their fields (t_valid, t_invalid, t_expired, embedding Vec<f32>, is_pinned) survive a JSON round-trip correctly. An ArchivePak with real Fact/Edge payloads that exercises all four bi-temporal timestamps (including None variants for t_expired, t_valid, t_invalid) would catch regressions from serde attribute changes on those types.
suggested_fix: Extend the inline test with a non-empty pak using fully-populated Fact and Edge values. Alternatively, or additionally, add a proptest that generates arbitrary Fact values (proptest is already a dev-dependency and used in src/store/facts.rs:1425) and asserts serde_json::from_str(serde_json::to_string(x)) == x for ArchivePak.

title: No property-based tests for ArchivePak encode/decode roundtrip despite proptest already in dev-deps
description: The codebase already uses proptest in src/store/facts.rs:1425, src/search/hybrid.rs:493, src/search/vector.rs:268, src/scope/tree.rs:311, and src/store/schema.rs. The archive module has a strong candidate for proptest: the decode(encode(x)) == x invariant for ArchivePak serialized through zstd+JSON (pak.rs:23-65). The existing write_read_roundtrip test at pak.rs:120 uses only a single hardcoded fixture. A proptest over arbitrary (pak_version, engine_schema_version, embed_dim, facts, edges) would catch field-level serde regressions and dimension mismatches.

title: read_pak has no fuzz target — cold-storage bytes from disk are parsed without fuzz coverage
description: read_pak (pak.rs:58) decompresses a zstd stream and then deserializes JSON from it. It is the only function in the codebase that accepts bytes originating from disk storage (i.e., potentially tampered or corrupted .pak files). There is no fuzz/ directory in the workspace. CWE-409 (decompression from untrusted source) and CWE-20 (improper input validation in deserialization) are both relevant. The MAX_PAK_DECOMPRESSED_SIZE cap at pak.rs:64 is the main safety valve, and it is not covered by any test. Fuzzing read_pak is the highest-value fuzz candidate in the archive module because it combines two parsing layers (zstd + serde_json) with a size limit that must hold.

title: verify_archives error branches (missing file, hash mismatch on disk) have no integration test
description: The integration test archive_lifecycle_roundtrip (archive_test.rs:106-111) calls verify_archives only on a valid, intact pak and asserts verify[0].ok == true. The two error branches in engine/archive.rs (file not found at line 136-141, hash mismatch at line 282-291) are never triggered by any test. Specifically: (1) no test removes a .pak after archival and then calls verify_archives to confirm ok=false with 'file not found'; (2) no test modifies a .pak file on disk and then calls verify_archives to confirm ok=false with 'hash mismatch'.

title: `check_error_keyword` assistant+bug-context branch has no test
description: The second branch of `check_error_keyword` fires when `"error"` appears in assistant text AND the assistant text also contains one of `["fix", "bug", "issue"]`. Only the stderr branch (line 418-419) is covered by `keyword_match_bug_error_in_stderr`. A turn such as `assistant: "There is an error in the fix"` with no tool stderr would exercise the uncovered branch; currently it goes untested.

title: Naive timestamp fallback path in `parse_timestamp` is untested
description: `parse_timestamp` tries RFC 3339 first then falls back to `%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S` (no timezone, treated as UTC). The only `parse_timestamp_valid` test uses `"2026-03-19T10:30:00Z"` which succeeds on the first branch. The fallback for timezone-less strings — which real Claude Code JSONL might emit — is never exercised.

title: `ContentBlock::ToolResult` arm in `parse_content_blocks` is not unit-tested
description: The inline unit tests cover `Text`, `ToolUse`, and `Thinking` blocks (parse.rs:271-300) but not the `"tool_result"` branch. This branch also has a content-extraction sub-branch: when `content` is a JSON string it extracts as-is, when it is any other JSON value it falls back to `v.to_string()`. Both sub-branches are untested.

title: `mixed_session.jsonl` fixture exists but is never referenced by any test
description: `tests/fixtures/mixed_session.jsonl` contains the only fixture that exercises `thinking` blocks, `progress`-type entries (noise filtering), Decision and Learning categories in the same session, and UUID-to-UUID pairing through a turn that skips over progress noise. It is confirmed unused by every `tests/*.rs` file. The three scenarios it covers are therefore integration-tested only superficially through the simpler fixtures.
suggested_fix: Add a test that includes `mixed_session.jsonl` via `include_str!`. Assert: `entries_parsed > 0`, thinking-block text does NOT surface as user or assistant text (verify the category is Learning or Convention from the keywords, not an artifact of thinking block leakage), and at least one Decision or Learning episode is found (`category_counts.decision + category_counts.learning > 0`).

title: Property-based test missing for `build_content` multi-byte truncation invariant
description: `build_content` contains a manual `char_boundary` walk-back loop (lines 120-122) to avoid cutting mid-codepoint. This is exactly the class of code that proptest catches: a test using ASCII-only input (`"a".repeat(3000)`) cannot find a 4-byte codepoint straddling position 2000. The invariant `output.len() <= MAX_LEN + 3 && output.is_char_boundary(output.len())` should hold for all UTF-8 content. `proptest` is already a workspace dependency.

title: No fuzz target for `parse_session_file` on adversarial JSONL bytes
description: The bootstrap pipeline entry point ingests untrusted JSONL (real session log files, or files passed via the MCP bootstrap endpoint). `parse_session_file` and `parse_content_blocks` are the first functions to touch that data. There is no `fuzz/` directory in the workspace, so no fuzzer has ever run against these parsers. The `serde_json` deserialization of `SessionEntry` and the `parse_single_block` match on unrecognized `type` strings are the highest-value targets. CWE-20 (Improper Input Validation).

title: truncate_str returns string longer than max_chars when max_chars < 3
description: When max_chars < 3 and the input string is longer than max_chars, truncate_str takes max_chars.saturating_sub(3) = 0 characters, then appends '...' (3 chars), returning a 3-char string that exceeds max_chars. Example: truncate_str("hello", 2) returns "..." (3 chars), violating the documented contract. The function is called with hardcoded values 60 and 80 in production, so no live breakage, but the contract is untested and the invariant is silently broken for small inputs.

title: dump 'all' target and dump JSON format have no integration test coverage
description: cli_integration.rs tests dump facts (table) and dump events (table) but never exercises `dump all` (the combined JSON branch at dump.rs:73-77) or the JSON output format for dump facts/events. The `dump_all` function builds a custom serde_json::json! object whose structure is different from individual list endpoints — an untested code path.

title: inspect and explain JSON/plain output formats have no integration test coverage
description: The existing test inspect_existing_fact only exercises the default Table format. explain_fact also only exercises Table. Both commands have Json and Plain branches that are untested. The Plain branch for inspect (line 106) emits only the content string, which is structurally different from Table and Json.

title: query --fact-type, --scope, --min-importance, --pinned-only filters have no CLI integration test coverage
description: The integration tests exercise query FTS text search and --valid-at, but none of --fact-type, --scope, --min-importance, or --pinned-only filters are exercised as actual CLI invocations. The fact_type string matching block (query.rs:90-98) with its error branch ('unknown fact type') is also untested.
suggested_fix:
Add tests that:
1. Pass `--fact-type semantic` and assert only semantic facts appear.
2. Pass `--fact-type unknown` and assert failure with 'unknown fact type' in stderr.
3. Pass `--pinned-only` to an empty-pinned DB and assert 'No results'.
4. Pass `--min-importance 0.99` on a DB with default-importance facts and assert 'No results'.

title: batch_ingest mid-stream batch flush path is never exercised by tests
description: All four inline tests of ingest_from_reader pass batch_size=100 with at most 2 facts, so the mid-stream flush branch (batch.len() >= batch_size, line 230) is never triggered. Only the final partial-batch flush (line 248-259) runs. A flush failure mid-stream (failed_batches += 1) is also untested.

title: ingest_from_reader all-bad-lines error path is untested
description: The bail at line 269 triggers when total_ingested==0 && total_skipped>0. No test exercises this path. The empty-input test (ingest_empty_input) skips it because total_skipped is also 0. A JSONL file containing only malformed or invalid lines should produce this error, but no test asserts on it.

title: Untrusted JSONL and JSON snapshot parsing have no fuzz targets
description: Two hot deserialization paths accept arbitrary bytes from external files: (1) serde_json::from_str on each JSONL line in ingest_from_reader (batch_ingest.rs:213) — a user-supplied file, potentially adversarial. (2) serde_json::from_reader in import::peek_embed_dim (import.rs:52) — reads arbitrary JSON from a snapshot file. Neither has a fuzz target. cargo-fuzz is not present in the workspace.

title: NotFound error path for nonexistent old_fact_id is untested
