title: Six `.iter().map(|x| x.id).collect::<Vec<_>>()` allocations feeding `reset_autoincrement` that only calls `.max()`
description:
The six `reset_autoincrement` call sites at lines 358-391 each allocate a temporary `Vec<i64>` only so `reset_autoincrement` can call `.iter().copied().max()`. The callers own the slice already; there is no need to materialize a new `Vec`.

Current state:
```rust
reset_autoincrement(&tx, "facts",
    &snapshot.facts.iter().map(|f| f.id).collect::<Vec<_>>())?;
```
Target state: change `reset_autoincrement` to accept `max_id: i64` directly (the callers compute `snapshot.facts.iter().map(|f| f.id).max().unwrap_or(0)`) — or make the signature `impl IntoIterator<Item = i64>` with no intermediate `Vec`.
Refactoring pattern: Introduce Parameter Object / eliminate intermediate collection.
Motivation: avoids six transient heap allocations at restore time; simpler call sites.
Estimated scope: 1 function + 6 call sites, all in `src/inspect/restore.rs`.
Prerequisites: none.
Risk: negligible.

title: Seven get_*/parse_* helpers are free functions in tools/mod.rs — should be a dedicated args-parsing module or struct
description: Current state: `get_str`, `get_i64`, `get_f64`, `get_bool`, `get_usize`, `get_datetime`, `get_depth`, `parse_embedding`, `parse_search_mode`, `parse_event_type`, `parse_fact_type`, `require_f64_if_present`, and `ok_json` — 13 helpers — are all private free functions in `tools/mod.rs`. Target state: extract to `tools/args.rs` and re-export into the handler files as needed. Alternatively, define a thin newtype `struct ToolArgs<'a>(&'a Map<String, Value>)` with methods, allowing `.get_str("key")` chaining instead of `get_str(&args, "key")`. Refactoring pattern: Extract Module / Introduce Parameter Object. Motivation: readability — the 90 LOC of helpers separates the schema section from the handlers and obscures the dispatch function; testability — the helpers could be unit-tested without constructing full handler inputs. Estimated scope: ~90 LOC movement, no logic change. Prerequisites: none. Risk: LOW.

title: embed_dim stored in ConnectionPool with #[allow(dead_code)] — pool owns data it does not use
description:
Current state: `ConnectionPool` stores `embed_dim: usize` (line 24) annotated with `#[allow(dead_code)]` (line 23) per comment "complete pool API — used after #108 engine split". The pool never validates or uses this field — it is just pass-through storage for `MemoryEngine`, which also stores `embed_dim` independently. The `embed_dim()` getter (line 229) is similarly suppressed.

Target state: remove `embed_dim` from `ConnectionPool` until issue #108 lands and the pool genuinely needs it. `MemoryEngine` already owns the value. The `#[allow(dead_code)]` annotation is a code smell that signals premature state accumulation.

Refactoring pattern: Remove premature API / extract when needed.
Motivation: coupling reduction, clarity (pool should not carry data for future users).
Estimated scope: `connection_pool.rs` — remove field + getter; update 3 open constructors.
Prerequisites: confirm `embed_dim()` is not called from any non-test site (confirmed: only test at line 307 calls it).
Risk: low — removal of an unused field; no behavioral change. When #108 lands, re-add.

title: resume_context fully deserializes embedding BLOBs for every returned fact even though the resume path does not use embeddings
description: Current state: all four `FactStore` methods called by `resume_context` (`list_pinned`, `list_by_importance_score`, `list_due`, `list_by_scopes_recent`) go through `row_to_fact` (`facts.rs:815-867`) which always deserializes the embedding BLOB (`deserialize_embedding`, line 837) into `Vec<f32>`. The resume path surfaces facts for context injection — it needs `content`, `importance_score`, timestamps, `is_pinned`, `fact_type`, and `scope_id`, but never the embedding. At DIM=768 each fact costs ~3 KB of deserialized float data. Target state: introduce a lightweight projection type (`FactSummary` or similar, without `embedding: Vec<f32>`) and dedicated query paths for the resume tier, analogous to how `SessionFact` (`facts.rs:808-813`) already strips embeddings for the session-edge path. Refactoring pattern: Query Projection / Lightweight DTO. Motivation: perf — resume_context is on the hot path at session start; at `pinned_cap=50 + high_importance_cap=20 + due_cap=10 + recent_cap=10 = 90 facts`, this is ~270 KB of allocation that is immediately discarded. Also readability: callers will see clearly which paths need embeddings and which do not. Estimated scope: 3 files (`context.rs`, `store/facts.rs`, `types.rs`). Prerequisites: the new projection type must not break `ResumeContext`'s serde round-trip (consumers may expect `embedding` in the returned `Fact`). Risk: medium — requires a public type change or a new public type; must audit all consumers of `ResumeContext::pinned`, `.high_importance`, `.due`, `.recent`.

title: scope_ids→JSON serialization repeated four times across three files
description: The pattern `scope_ids.map(|ids| serde_json::to_string(ids).expect("..."))` appears verbatim four times with slightly different error messages. Current state: four inline one-liners, each with a different string literal in `expect()`. Target state: a single `pub(crate) fn scope_ids_to_json(scope_ids: Option<&[i64]>) -> Option<String>` in a shared location (e.g., `search/mod.rs` or `store/facts.rs`). Refactoring pattern: Extract Function. Motivation: DRY, consistent error message, single location to change if the encoding changes. Estimated scope: 3 files changed, ~8 lines net reduction. Prerequisites: none. Risk: low — trivial substitution.

title: Non-atomic temp-file creation on a predictable path (symlink/TOCTOU) — File::create follows and truncates
description: write_pak_and_hash creates the temp file with `fs::File::create(&tmp_path)` (pak.rs:26) where `tmp_path = path.with_extension("pak.tmp")` (pak.rs:24). The destination filename is fully predictable: engine/archive.rs:200 generates `archive-{yyyymmddhhmmss}-{nanos:08x}.pak`, so the .pak.tmp name is guessable. `fs::File::create` opens O_CREAT|O_TRUNC and FOLLOWS symlinks. In a shared/multi-user archive_dir, an attacker who pre-creates `archive-...-....pak.tmp` as a symlink to a sensitive file causes that target to be truncated and overwritten with zstd-JSON at open time; the downstream atomic `fs::rename` (pak.rs:47) does not mitigate this because the damage occurs at open. Severity is low because the library is normally single-user in-process, but the audit's TOCTOU/temp-path category explicitly prescribes atomic create_new / tempfile, and the fix is one line.

title: Operator-supplied --batch-size flows unvalidated into Vec::with_capacity
description: `BatchIngestArgs.batch_size` (CLI flag `--batch-size`, default 100) is a `usize` with no upper bound, and is passed straight to `Vec::with_capacity(batch_size)` at batch_ingest.rs:194. An invocation such as `--batch-size 18446744073709551615` triggers an immediate huge up-front allocation request (capacity-overflow abort or OOM). Severity is low because the value is operator-controlled (the operator owns their own invocation, not a remote attacker), but it is an unvalidated CLI numeric flowing into a sizing primitive with no sanity clamp. CWE-789.
suggested_fix:
Clamp/validate at the top of `run` (or via clap `value_parser` with a range):

    anyhow::ensure!((1..=100_000).contains(&args.batch_size),
        "--batch-size must be in 1..=100000, got {}", args.batch_size);

or on the field: `#[arg(long, default_value = "100", value_parser = clap::value_parser!(usize).range(1..=100_000))]`.

title: Bearer API key accepted as a plain command-line flag (process-arg / shell-history exposure)
description: `--embed-api-key` is exposed as a plain `Option<String>` clap argument. When an operator passes the bearer secret on the command line, it is written into the process argument vector — readable by any local user via `ps` or `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` for the lifetime of the process — and persisted into shell history. The safer env-var form (`MEMORY_ENGINE_EMBED_API_KEY`) already exists on the same field, but the flag form remains available and is the path most operators reach for. CWE-214 (invocation of process with sensitive data on command line), CWE-532.
suggested_fix: Prefer steering secrets to the env var / a key file rather than the flag. Options: (1) document and emit a stderr warning when the key arrives via the CLI flag rather than the env var; (2) accept the key only via env var or a `--embed-api-key-file <path>` that reads the secret from a file with restrictive perms; (3) at minimum keep the env-var form as the documented default and de-emphasize the inline flag in help text. clap cannot mask an already-passed arg, so the real fix is removing/deprecating the inline-secret path.

title: Consumer-supplied embedding written to store without dimension validation
description: generator.embed(...) returns a Vec<f32> of arbitrary length that is passed directly into summary_store.insert(&NewSummary { embedding: summary_embedding, .. }) at cluster.rs:87 and global.rs:71 with no check that its length equals embed_dim. The store serializes it verbatim (serialize_embedding, store/mod.rs:27) with no dim guard on write. The mismatch is only self-detected on the NEXT read: deserialize_embedding (store/mod.rs:46) enforces blob.len()==dim*4 and returns MemoryError::EmbeddingDimension, which means list_by_level / row_to_summary will then fail for that level until the corrupt row is manually removed — a latent data-integrity / availability foot-gun rather than a memory-safety issue (no unsafe, so no OOB). summary_text length is likewise unbounded but lower risk. Trusting trait output read back as if validated is the CWE-20 shape.
suggested_fix: Validate before insert. After `let summary_embedding = generator.embed(&summary_text)?;` add: `if summary_embedding.len() != embed_dim { return Err(crate::error::MemoryError::EmbeddingDimension { expected: embed_dim, actual: summary_embedding.len() }); }` in both cluster.rs and global.rs. This fails fast inside the transaction (rolling back) instead of writing a blob that breaks future reads.

title: serde_json::Value payload/metadata fields are an under-bounded trust boundary (CWE-502/CWE-20/CWE-400)
description: The core types derive Serialize+Deserialize and are explicitly the snapshot/restore and DB-readback format (types.rs:236-246 LineageSnapshotEntry 'snapshot dump/restore'; restored via serde_json::from_reader at src/inspect/restore.rs:86 and from_str across src/store/*). Several fields are typed serde_json::Value with no schema or size validation at the type level: Event.payload (types.rs:95), Fact.metadata (types.rs:136), AddFactOptions.metadata (types.rs:259), Insight.metadata (types.rs:376), PromoteRequest.metadata (types.rs:493), NewActivity.args/Activity.args (types.rs:532), SessionCheckpoint.metadata/RecordActivityRequest.args (types.rs:564,576). After deserialization these blobs are treated as validated and re-emitted/queried downstream. Severity is LOW, not higher, because serde_json 1.0.149 enforces a default ~128-level recursion limit on from_str/from_slice/from_reader, which mitigates the classic deeply-nested-JSON stack-overflow DoS (CWE-776/CWE-674) for these fields without action here. The residual risk is breadth/total-size: a very large or very wide Value (not deep) in a malicious .pak/JSON snapshot is unbounded and is loaded fully into memory. This is a hardening gap on an untrusted-input boundary, not an exploitable memory-safety hole.
suggested_fix: Treat snapshot/restore JSON as untrusted: (1) impose a total-document byte cap before parsing in the restore path (e.g. wrap the reader in a length-limited reader), and (2) optionally validate Value shape/size for payload/metadata after deserialize (reject objects/arrays exceeding a configured element budget). Document in the type that the recursion limit is the parser's, and that callers restoring third-party snapshots must size-cap input. No type signature change is mechanically safe, so this needs a human decision on the budget.

title: Embedding and id-list Vec fields deserialize without a length cap (CWE-400/CWE-770)
description: Fact.embedding/NewFact.embedding/Summary.embedding/PromoteRequest.embedding are Vec<f32> (types.rs:126,162,318,489) and source_fact_ids/representative_ids/Summary.source_fact_ids are Vec<i64> (types.rs:164,214,227,234,244,497). These derive Deserialize with no length bound and are loaded from snapshots/DB blobs (src/store/lineage.rs:117,207 and summaries.rs:188 deserialize Vec<i64> straight from DB text). The engine validates embedding dimension against embed_dim elsewhere (error.rs:13 EmbeddingDimension), but that check is downstream of deserialization and not all Vec fields are dimension-checked (e.g. source_fact_ids). Because the wire format is JSON (no length-prefix), there is no length-field amplification: allocation is bounded by actual input bytes, which is why this is LOW rather than a classic CWE-789 untrusted-allocation. It remains a hardening gap: a large hostile snapshot causes proportional large allocation with no per-field ceiling, and an embedding Vec restored at the wrong length only fails later when dimension is checked, not at the deserialization boundary.
suggested_fix: Validate Vec lengths immediately after restore: reject Fact/Summary/NewFact whose embedding.len() != engine embed_dim before insertion, and cap source_fact_ids/representative_ids to a sane maximum (e.g. a few thousand) in the restore/import path. Pair with the document-level byte cap from core-root/deserialization-value-trust-boundary. Choosing the caps requires human judgement, so not auto-fixable.

title: Embedding array deserialized into Vec<f32> before expected_dim validation
description: The embedding arrays are materialized via `serde_json::from_value::<Vec<f32>>(...)` (embed: lines 148/155; parse_openai_batch: lines 64-71; parse_ollama_batch: line 105) BEFORE any length check against `expected_dim` (which is only enforced afterward at lines 167 and 234). A server can return an array with an arbitrary number of elements; the full Vec<f32> is allocated and only then rejected for dimension mismatch. This is distinct from and not covered by the body-size cap (embed/dos-unbounded-response-body): even within a capped body, the post-parse allocation is an independent step worth bounding by checking the array length on the serde_json::Value first. Severity is low because Vec<f32> is smaller than the parsed Value tree (so it is dominated by the body cap), but it is a cheap, precise hardening step.

title: from_snapshot trusts deserialized edge fields (source/target/edge_id/weight) without revalidating against the DB
description: from_snapshot copies source, target, edge_id, relation_type, and weight directly out of each GraphEdgeSnapshot into the in-memory graph with no validation that these correspond to real, active edges in the SQLite store. The DB fingerprint check (engine/snapshot.rs:333) only compares aggregate counts (active_edge_count, max_edge_id, etc.), not the per-edge content. A tampered .snapshot that preserves those aggregate counts (e.g. same number of edges but different endpoints/relation_types) passes the fingerprint and blake3 (since the attacker recomputes the hash over their payload — blake3 is unkeyed) and silently installs a divergent in-memory graph: bogus edges, wrong relation types, or edges between fact ids that do not exist as active facts. Because the graph drives importance scoring (degree), neighbor traversal, and connected_component, this corrupts downstream consolidation/forgetting decisions without any audit trail. This is the classic 'trust data read back from a store as if it were validated' problem (CWE-20/CWE-502); the same trust gap exists for the scope tree snapshot.
suggested_fix: Treat the snapshot as a cache, not a source of truth, for integrity-sensitive fields. Either (a) make the DbFingerprint cover edge content (e.g. include a rolling hash of (id, source, target, relation_type) over active edges, computed in read_fingerprint, so any per-edge tamper invalidates the snapshot and forces load_from_db), or (b) on load, validate that each (edge_id) referenced by the snapshot exists and is active in the edges table before trusting it. Given the sidecar already falls back to load_from_db on any mismatch, option (a) is the cheaper and more robust fix and closes the gap for the scope tree snapshot too.

title: VACUUM INTO target path silently lossy-converted via to_string_lossy before SQL escaping
description: dump_sqlite builds the VACUUM INTO target with `path.to_string_lossy().replace('\'', "''")` (dump.rs:213) then format!("VACUUM INTO '{escaped}'") (dump.rs:219). On a non-UTF-8 path, to_string_lossy replaces invalid byte sequences with U+FFFD, so the SQL string no longer designates the intended file: the dump can land at an unexpected path or fail confusingly. The single-quote doubling and the null-byte rejection (dump.rs:214) are correct mitigations against quote-breakout, and SQLite genuinely cannot bind a VACUUM INTO target as a parameter, so the format! itself is acceptable; the residual issue is the silent lossy conversion of the path, not injection. CWE-22-adjacent / CWE-116 (improper encoding). Low because the caller controls the path (not typically untrusted) and quote-injection is already blocked.

title: Several tools accept unbounded result counts / input payloads from untrusted clients
description: memory_query forwards an arbitrary client-chosen `limit` (any usize, line 727) to the engine, and memory_replay_events treats `limit: 0` as 'no limit' (line 1174) — both let a client request an unbounded result set that the engine materializes into Vecs. memory_flush_insights iterates a client array of arbitrary length (line 855) and memory_bootstrap_session takes `jsonl_data` as a String then re-materializes it via .into_bytes() into a Cursor (line 1239), doubling peak memory of an already-unbounded payload. None of these have an upper bound at the MCP boundary; max_turns (bootstrap) caps processed turns but not the raw input size. These are DoS amplification vectors (CWE-400) against a server exposed to untrusted MCP clients. The replay limit=0 case is a documented operator convenience that becomes dangerous when the server faces an untrusted client.
suggested_fix: Clamp client-supplied limits to a server-side maximum (e.g. let limit = get_usize(&args,"limit").unwrap_or(10).min(MAX_QUERY_LIMIT)) and disallow / cap the replay 'unbounded' path when serving untrusted clients. Reject flush_insights arrays and jsonl_data above a configured byte/element cap (e.g. if jsonl_data.len() > MAX_BOOTSTRAP_BYTES { return invalid_params }). Make these caps configurable in McpConfig so operators can tune them.

title: read() blocks indefinitely with no timeout; a leaked ReadGuard deadlocks all readers (CWE-400)
description: `read()` checks out a pooled connection via `while conns.is_empty() { self.read_available.wait(&mut conns); }` (lines 195-197). The `while`-loop correctly guards against spurious wakeups, so this is not a correctness bug. However there is no bounded wait: if all `read_pool_size` connections are checked out and one `ReadGuard` is leaked (e.g. `mem::forget`, a guard stored in a long-lived struct, or a slow/hung query holding a connection) the remaining callers block on the Condvar forever with no timeout and no error path. This is an availability/liveness hazard (unbounded wait / potential deadlock fan-out across all readers) rather than memory unsafety. CWE-400 (Uncontrolled Resource Consumption).
suggested_fix: Use a bounded wait and surface exhaustion as a recoverable error instead of an unbounded block, e.g.: `let timeout = std::time::Duration::from_secs(30); while conns.is_empty() { if self.read_available.wait_for(&mut conns, timeout).timed_out() && conns.is_empty() { return Err(MemoryError::PoolTimeout); } }` (requires a new error variant and changing `read()` to return `Result<ReadConn<'_>>`). At minimum, document the deadlock-on-leak contract on `read()`.

title: Unchecked integer multiplication on consumer-controlled limit in HNSW overfetch
description: In `HnswStrategy::search`, `overfetch` is derived from the consumer-controlled `limit` via plain (non-checked) multiplication: `let mut overfetch = limit * OVERFETCH_FACTOR;` (line 238) and then `overfetch *= 2;` (line 295) inside the widen loop (up to MAX_WIDEN_ATTEMPTS=3 iterations). `limit` originates from `MemoryQuery::limit(n)` (src/search/query.rs:223) and is propagated unmodified through `MemoryEngine::execute_query` -> `effective_limit()` -> `SearchQuery.limit` -> `hybrid_search` -> the strategy `search` call; there is NO upper-bound clamp anywhere on this path (verified src/engine/query.rs:119). With a large `limit` (near `usize::MAX`, or `>= usize::MAX/3` then doubled), `limit * OVERFETCH_FACTOR` and the subsequent `overfetch *= 2` overflow: in debug builds this panics (CWE-190 unexpected abort), in release builds it silently wraps to a small/incorrect value, degrading recall. Note the downstream allocation is NOT the blast radius -- `dest_len = overfetch.min(n_items)` (line 254) clamps the `vec![Neighbor; dest_len]` to the indexed item count, so this is a wrapping/panic semantics bug, not an unbounded-allocation OOM. In the sibling `hybrid.rs` path the analogous arithmetic correctly uses `effective_target.saturating_mul(3)` (src/search/hybrid.rs:150), so the unchecked form here is an inconsistency. This code is behind the `ann` feature and is lint-blind (--all-features broken per audit scope), so clippy::arithmetic_side_effects would not have flagged it.

title: Silent u16 wrapping in upcaster revision arithmetic (from_revision + 1)
description: UpcasterRegistry::register computes `let target = from_revision + 1;` where `from_revision: u16`. `register` is part of the crate's public API (consumer-facing trait wiring). With overflow-checks OFF in release builds (no `overflow-checks = true` is set in any workspace Cargo.toml, so release uses the default of OFF), a consumer registering an upcaster with `from_revision == u16::MAX` (65535) makes `target` wrap to 0 instead of panicking. The corrupted `latest` revision then mis-drives the upcast loop bound at upcaster.rs:90/98 (`current_revision >= latest` / `while rev < latest`). This is a contrived input (revisions are small monotonic counters), hence low severity, but it is genuine release-mode silent wraparound in index/version arithmetic. CWE-190.
suggested_fix: Use checked or saturating arithmetic: `let target = from_revision.checked_add(1).ok_or_else(|| MemoryError::Migration(format!("upcaster from_revision {from_revision} would overflow u16")))?;` (requires changing the signature to return Result), or minimally `let target = from_revision.saturating_add(1);` to make the wrap impossible.

title: DB-stored JSON deserialized with unwrap_or_default(), silently masking corruption
description: Two row-mapping functions deserialize JSON columns read back from SQLite using `serde_json::from_str(&s).unwrap_or_default()`: `row_to_activity` (activities.rs:218, the `args` column) and `row_to_checkpoint` (checkpoints.rs:98, the `metadata` column). On malformed stored JSON this silently substitutes `serde_json::Value::Null` instead of surfacing an error. This trusts blobs/JSON read back from the DB as if validated and defeats the schema's own `CHECK(json_valid(args))` / `CHECK(json_valid(metadata))` guarantees (schema.rs:672, 699): if a row ever reaches an invalid state (e.g. via raw SQL restore path, a future migration, or a manually-edited DB file), the data corruption is hidden rather than detected. Every other row mapper in the module propagates the error properly via `map_err(...)` (see facts.rs:841-843, summaries.rs:188-190), so these two are an inconsistency that weakens the input-validation posture. CWE-20.
suggested_fix: Propagate the error like the sibling mappers. e.g. activities.rs:218: `let args: serde_json::Value = serde_json::from_str(&args_str).map_err(|e| rusqlite::Error::FromSqlConversionFailure(4, rusqlite::types::Type::Text, Box::new(e)))?;` and the analogous change at checkpoints.rs:98 (column index 5).

title: `write_pak` suppresses `dead_code` instead of being removed or made `pub(crate)`
description: Current state: `write_pak` at pak.rs:15-19 carries `#[allow(dead_code)]` with a comment 'Used in unit tests below; restore tooling will also use this.' It is used only in the `#[cfg(test)]` block below it. If it is only a test utility, it should be gated with `#[cfg(test)]`. If it is intended for future restore tooling, the `#[allow(dead_code)]` suppression silently hides the fact that the planned caller does not exist yet, and the comment is the only signal. Target state: either (a) move `write_pak` inside `#[cfg(test)]` next to its only callers, or (b) leave it in production code and track the missing restore-tooling caller via a `#[doc(hidden)]` note or a `TODO` comment rather than suppressing the lint. Refactoring pattern: Remove Dead Code / Test-Scope Gating. Motivation: lint hygiene; dead production code is a maintenance liability. Estimated scope: 1 file (pak.rs). Prerequisites: none. Risk: none if (a); if (b), only cosmetic.

title: `&Option<String>` parameters should be `Option<&str>`
description: Current state: `jsonl_to_request(fact: JsonlFact, default_scope: &Option<String>)` (line 122) and `ingest_from_reader(..., default_scope: &Option<String>, ...)` (line 185) take a reference to an owned Option instead of an Option of a reference. The idiomatic Rust form for borrowing an optional string is `Option<&str>`. With `&Option<String>`, callers must pass `&args.scope` (awkward) and the function body must call `.clone()` to produce the owned `Option<String>` needed downstream (line 136: `default_scope.clone()`). With `Option<&str>`, the clone becomes `.map(str::to_owned)` at the one site that needs it. Refactoring pattern: Replace Borrowed Container with Inner Borrow. Motivation: idiomatic API, avoids unnecessary clone, clippy `clippy::ref_option` lint. Scope: 1 file, 2 function signatures + 2 call sites. Prerequisites: none. Risk: none — mechanical.

title: unchecked_transaction() called three times without a safety rationale comment
description: Current state: `conn.unchecked_transaction()` is called on lines 79, 116, and 152 with no comment. `unchecked_transaction` bypasses rusqlite's lifetime guard against nested transactions; it is the correct call when the function receives a `&Connection` (not a `Transaction`), but silence makes reviewers wonder why `transaction()` was not used instead. Target state: a one-line `// SAFETY: conn is not nested inside another transaction at this call site` comment before each call, or a single shared note in the module doc. Refactoring pattern: Add Safety Comment. Motivation: future reviewers spending time re-deriving why `unchecked_transaction` is safe here instead of `transaction()`. Estimated scope: 1 file, 3 lines. Risk: none. LIGHT: mechanical.

title: remove_edges_for_fact is a one-line passthrough wrapper adding no clarity
description: Current state: `remove_edges_for_fact` (lines 205-207) consists of a single forwarding call `graph.remove_edges_by_fact(fact_id)`. It is called from two places: `rebuild_graph_for_fact` (line 192) and the `Delete` arm (line 164). Target state: inline the call to `graph.remove_edges_by_fact(fact_id)` directly at both call sites, eliminating the wrapper. The function name adds no information over the graph method name. Refactoring pattern: Inline Method. Motivation: an indirection that carries no abstraction value increases the cognitive load of tracing call chains. Estimated scope: 1 file. Risk: none. LIGHT: mechanical inline.

title: resolve_conflict body is 138 lines, exceeding the 60-LOC guideline
description: Current state: `resolve_conflict` spans lines 35-173 (138 lines including the `match` block and helpers called inline). The 60-LOC threshold from the audit scope is exceeded. The excess is largely the three transaction arms. Target state: after applying the Extract Method refactoring (finding conflict/refactoring-transaction-arm-duplication), the function body would collapse to ~50 lines (arbiter call + 4-arm match delegating to extracted helpers). Motivation: readability and ease of code review. Estimated scope: 1 file. Prerequisites: the transaction-arm-duplication refactoring. Risk: LOW if done after extracting helpers. HEAVY: requires the prior refactoring as a prerequisite.
suggested_fix: Apply conflict/refactoring-transaction-arm-duplication first; the function length violation resolves as a consequence.

title: Transaction-level 'now' timestamp not threaded through all passes — each pass calls Utc::now() independently
description: Current state: `mod.rs:48` computes `let now = Utc::now()` before the transaction opens, and passes it to `local_dedup`. However `cluster_fusion` (cluster.rs:93 `created_at: chrono::Utc::now()`) and `global_integration` (global.rs:77 `created_at: chrono::Utc::now()`) each call `Utc::now()` independently. All three passes are inside one SQLite transaction, yet summary timestamps can differ by milliseconds from the dedup timestamp. Target state: pass `now: DateTime<Utc>` into all three pass functions for consistent timestamps within the atomically-committed consolidation run. This also makes tests deterministic. Refactoring pattern: Lift Shared Value to Caller / Thread Context Through API. Motivation: temporal consistency (the transaction is atomic; timestamps should be too), testability (injectable `now`). Scope: 3 files. Prerequisites: none. Risk: low.

title: Individual pass functions re-exported as pub but only consumed within the consolidation module
description: Current state: `mod.rs` re-exports `cluster_fusion`, `local_dedup`, and `global_integration` as `pub use` (lines 9-11). The parent module in lib.rs is `pub(crate) mod consolidation`, so these are effectively `pub(crate)`. However the only consumer is the `consolidate()` function in the same file — the passes are never called from outside `consolidation/`. Making them `pub` (even bounded to `pub(crate)` via the parent) allows other engine modules to call them in isolation, bypassing the orchestrator and its watermark/transaction logic. Target state: remove the `pub use` re-exports; reference the submodule items as `cluster::cluster_fusion`, `dedup::local_dedup`, `global::global_integration` directly within `consolidate()`, keeping them at their natural `pub(super)` (or even private) visibility. Refactoring pattern: Reduce Visibility. Motivation: encapsulation (prevents accidental direct invocations that skip the transaction), API surface minimality. Scope: 1 file (mod.rs), with adjustments to the three submodule function declarations from `pub fn` to `pub(super) fn`). Prerequisites: none. Risk: low.

title: Five-parameter positional constructor is prone to argument-order mistakes
description: Current state: `HttpEmbeddingProvider::new(endpoint: String, model: String, api_key: Option<String>, expected_dim: usize, timeout_secs: u64)`. `expected_dim` (usize) and `timeout_secs` (u64) are distinct only by type, but callers must remember the order. Target state: A `HttpEmbeddingProviderBuilder` (or at minimum, a config struct `HttpEmbeddingConfig { endpoint, model, api_key, expected_dim, timeout_secs }` passed to `new(config)`) makes construction self-documenting and prevents silent argument transposition. Refactoring pattern: Introduce Parameter Object / Builder. Motivation: misuse-resistance, readability. Estimated scope: 1 file + callsites in mcp + cli. Risk: low but breaks public API surface. Prerequisites: semver — crate is 0.1.0 so this is fine.

title: Two separate `impl HttpEmbeddingProvider` blocks with no structural reason for the split
description: Current state: The struct has two consecutive `impl HttpEmbeddingProvider` blocks — the first (lines 18–41) holds `new()`, the second (lines 43–113) holds the private parsing helpers. Target state: Merge into one `impl` block. The split implies a visibility distinction (e.g., `pub` vs private) that does not actually exist here — both blocks mix `pub` and private items. Refactoring pattern: Inline / Consolidate. Motivation: readability, conventional Rust style. Estimated scope: 1 file. Risk: none.
suggested_fix: // Remove the second `impl HttpEmbeddingProvider {` header and its closing `}`, joining both blocks.

title: `serde` not declared as a direct dependency despite using `serde_json::from_value` in public parsing helpers
description: Current state: `memory-engine-embed/Cargo.toml` declares `serde_json` but not `serde`. The `http.rs` file uses only `serde_json` APIs, so this compiles. However, if finding `embed/design-untyped-response-format` is implemented (introduce `#[derive(Deserialize)]` types), `serde` with `derive` feature will be needed and must be added explicitly. Currently this is not a bug but an incomplete dep declaration for future direction. Target state: Add `serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }` when typed response structs are introduced. Refactoring pattern: Dependency hygiene. Motivation: correctness of Cargo manifest. Risk: none today.
suggested_fix:
# In memory-engine-embed/Cargo.toml:
[dependencies]
serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
serde_json = "1"
# (add only when typed response deserialization is introduced)

title: ebbinghaus_decay and compute_importance are pub inside a pub(crate) module
description:
Current state: `ebbinghaus_decay` (line 22) and `compute_importance` (line 36) are declared `pub fn`. The enclosing module (`forgetting`) is `pub(crate)` (lib.rs:39), and `forgetting/mod.rs` only re-exports `prune` — so these two functions are already unreachable outside the crate by the module boundary. The `pub` annotation is misleading: it implies an intent to expose the function further than the module boundary permits.

Target state: Change both to `pub(crate)` (or `pub(super)` since only `mod.rs` needs them) to make visibility explicit and match the module's declared access level.

Refactoring pattern: Tighten Visibility.

Motivation: Readability — `pub` on something that cannot be reached from outside the crate creates a false expectation. Should the `forgetting` module ever be promoted to `pub`, these functions would be silently exposed.

Estimated scope: 1 file (policy.rs lines 22, 36). Prerequisites: none. Risk: NONE — purely a visibility qualifier change; behaviour and compilation are identical.

title: FREQUENCY_NORMALIZATION_CEILING and CONNECTIVITY_NORMALIZATION_CEILING hold ceiling+1, not the ceiling
description:
Current state:
```rust
const FREQUENCY_NORMALIZATION_CEILING: f64 = 101.0;  // doc says "100 accesses = full score"
const CONNECTIVITY_NORMALIZATION_CEILING: f64 = 51.0; // doc says "50 connections = full score"
```
The inline comments correctly state the semantic ceiling (100 / 50), but the constant values are ceiling+1 (101 / 51) because they are used as the argument to `ln()` alongside `ln_1p(count)`. The names claim "ceiling" while carrying "ceiling+1" — a reader tracing the formula must mentally subtract 1.

Target state: Either rename to reflect the actual stored value (`FREQUENCY_LN_NORMALIZATION_BASE = 101.0`) or store the true ceiling and compute `(ceiling + 1.0).ln()` at the use sites (one multiply per prune call — negligible cost). The latter keeps the constant semantically aligned with the doc comment.

Refactoring pattern: Rename Constant / Clarify Invariant.

Motivation: Readability — mismatch between name and value forces a mental decode step every time the formula is read. Any future tuning of the ceiling values will require updating both the constant and the inline comment, with no compiler enforcement that they stay consistent.

Estimated scope: 1 file (policy.rs lines 13, 16, 56, 59). Prerequisites: none. Risk: NONE.

title: prune returns an anonymous (PruneStats, Vec<i64>) tuple; the Vec<i64> is undocumented in the doc comment
description:
Current state: `prune` is declared `pub fn prune(...) -> Result<(PruneStats, Vec<i64>)>`. The doc comment (lines 79–81) documents `PruneStats` semantics but says nothing about the `Vec<i64>` (expired fact IDs). Callers must infer from the name `expired_ids` used at call sites.

Target state: Either (a) add a one-line `/// The second element is the list of fact IDs soft-deleted by this call.` to the existing doc comment — minimal, correct, low-risk; or (b) introduce a named `PruneResult { pub stats: PruneStats, pub expired_ids: Vec<i64> }` — eliminates positional ambiguity for any future tuple extension.

Refactoring pattern: Replace Tuple with Named Struct (option b) or Document Return Value (option a).

Motivation: Readability / misuse-resistance — the `Vec<i64>` positional slot is invisible at call sites. Option (a) is mechanical and sufficient; option (b) is the zero-ambiguity path if the return type ever grows.

Estimated scope: 1 file for option (a); 2–3 files for option (b) (policy.rs + engine/forgetting.rs + engine/cognitive.rs). Prerequisites: none. Risk: NONE for (a); LOW for (b).

title: remove_edge_by_id scans all edges O(E); documentation overstates multiplicity
description: Current state: `remove_edge_by_id` iterates all `edge_indices()` to find those whose `EdgeData.edge_id` matches the SQLite primary key (line 68-72). Since `edges.id` is a UNIQUE primary key, at most one edge matches — but the loop collects a `Vec` of potentially many and iterates it. The doc comment says "remove all edges", implying multiplicity that does not exist in the data model. This makes the function O(E) instead of O(1) with a secondary index. Target state: either (a) add a `HashMap<i64, EdgeIndex>` secondary index to `MemoryGraph` (same pattern as `node_map`) for O(1) lookup, or (b) at minimum, change the return type to `bool`/`Option<()>` and short-circuit after the first match. Option (b) is LIGHT; option (a) is MEDIUM. Estimated scope: 1 file. Prerequisites for (a): must handle `EdgeIndex` invalidation on `remove_edge` (same swap-remove issue applies — mitigation: re-use `StableDiGraph` from the blocker finding above, which preserves `EdgeIndex` too). Risk (b): NONE.

title: `fact.t_invalid.unwrap()` inside a short-circuit boolean guard instead of let-binding
description:
In `determine_state` at line 101:
```rust
if t_valid <= now && (fact.t_invalid.is_none() || fact.t_invalid.unwrap() > now) {
```
The `fact.t_invalid.unwrap()` is safe at runtime (the `is_none()` short-circuit prevents reaching it when the value is `None`), but it reads as a potential panic site to auditors and is not idiomatic. `Option::is_none_or` (stable since Rust 1.82) or `Option::map_or` eliminate the unwrap entirely.

Current state: `.unwrap()` called on `Option` under short-circuit guard.
Target state: replace with `fact.t_invalid.is_none_or(|t| t > now)` (1.82+) or `fact.t_invalid.map_or(true, |t| t > now)` for MSRV compatibility.
Refactoring pattern: Replace with combinator (clippy `option_if_let_else`).
Motivation: readability, no accidental panic.
Estimated scope: 1 line.
Prerequisites: none.
Risk: none.

title: Three sites use format!("{:?}", enum_val) to serialize enums — produces unstable Rust Debug output in JSON
description: Current state: `match_type`, `state`, and `kind` fields in shaped JSON are serialized via `format!("{:?}", ...)` — e.g. `json!(format!("{:?}", result.match_type))`. Debug output is not a stable contract: variant name formatting can change with Rust edition or derive changes. Target state: use `serde_json::to_value` or implement `Display` / `serde::Serialize` and use `json!(result.match_type)` directly. These types (`MatchType`, `FactState`, `HistoryEventKind`) already derive `Serialize` (they are core engine types). Refactoring pattern: Replace Debug Serialization with Serialize. Motivation: API stability — the JSON wire format seen by MCP clients should not be tied to Rust's Debug representation. Estimated scope: 3 call sites in `depth.rs`. Prerequisites: verify target types implement `Serialize`. Risk: LIGHT — output is functionally the same for simple enum variants, but becomes contract-stable.

title: Module doc claims 'bounded channel for readers' but implementation uses Mutex<Vec> + Condvar
description:
The module-level doc comment (`src/pool/mod.rs:3`) reads: "Uses `parking_lot::Mutex` for the write lock and a **bounded channel** for readers." The actual implementation (`connection_pool.rs:20-22`) uses `Mutex<Vec<Connection>>` + `Condvar` — there is no channel. This stale comment will confuse any contributor reasoning about the pool's internal concurrency model.

Target state: update the doc comment to accurately describe the Mutex+Condvar approach.
Refactoring pattern: Documentation correction.
Motivation: readability / onboarding accuracy.
Estimated scope: 1 line in 1 file.
Prerequisites: none.
Risk: none.
suggested_fix:
// src/pool/mod.rs:3
//! Uses `parking_lot::Mutex` for the write lock and a `Mutex<Vec<Connection>>` + `Condvar` for readers.

title: path.to_string_lossy() silently corrupts non-UTF-8 paths when opening connections
description:
Current state: four call sites convert `&Path` to `&str` via `path.to_string_lossy()` before passing to `store::schema::open_connection(path: &str)` / `open_connection_read_only(path: &str)`. `to_string_lossy()` replaces invalid UTF-8 sequences with U+FFFD, silently producing a different path string. On Windows with certain special characters or on Linux with non-UTF-8 filenames, this would open a different (or non-existent) file without error.

Root cause: `store::schema::open_connection` and `open_connection_read_only` accept `&str` rather than `&Path` / `impl AsRef<OsStr>`.

Target state: change `open_connection` and `open_connection_read_only` signatures to accept `&Path`. `rusqlite::Connection::open` already accepts `AsRef<Path>`, so no conversion would be needed at all.

Refactoring pattern: Widen parameter type from `&str` to `&Path`.
Motivation: correctness on non-UTF-8 paths, reduces conversion boilerplate.
Estimated scope: `store/schema.rs` (2 fn signatures) + 4 call sites in `connection_pool.rs` + any other callers of those schema functions.
Prerequisites: none.
Risk: low — strictly wider API; all call sites already have `&Path`.

title: Doc comment says 'Five tiers, mutually exclusive' but the mutual-exclusion invariant is vacuous for kb_stubs
description: Current state: the doc comment on `resume_context` (line 60) declares 'Five tiers, mutually exclusive (no fact appears in multiple tiers)' and lists `kb_stubs` as tier 5. But `kb_stubs` is `Vec<String>` (URIs, not `Fact`s), so the mutual-exclusion claim is meaningless for it, and there is no dedup logic that would apply. The comment implies a stronger contract than exists. Target state: reword to 'Four fact tiers, mutually exclusive … plus one placeholder tier (kb_stubs)'. Refactoring pattern: Doc Clarification. Motivation: documentation precision — misleading invariant descriptions erode trust in the spec. Scope: 1 file, doc text only. Risk: none.

title: Magic literal `1` for root scope ID repeated across methods
description: Current state: `root_id()` returns the bare literal `1i64` (line 39), and `resolve_path` restates it as `1i64` inline (line 45). Both `path_for_id` and `from_snapshot` also compare against `self.root_id()` (lines 151, 159) but that consistency was not carried back to `resolve_path`. Target state: extract `const ROOT_ID: i64 = 1;` as a `pub(crate)` associated constant (or module-level constant) and use it in all three sites. Pattern: Replace Magic Number with Constant. Motivation: readability, single point of change if the sentinel ever moves during bootstrapping. Scope: 1 file, 2–3 sites. Prerequisites: none. Risk: trivially zero — pure rename, no logic change.

title: No-op `.prop_map(|s| s)` identity closure in proptest helper
description: Current state: `scope_segment()` at line 314 applies `.prop_map(|s| s)`, which is a pure identity transform that clippy flags as `clippy::redundant_closure` (or `map_identity`). Target state: remove the `.prop_map(|s| s)` call entirely; the regex strategy already returns `Strategy<Value = String>`. Pattern: Remove Identity Closure. Motivation: readability. Scope: 1 line. Prerequisites: none. Risk: zero.

title: HNSW_SEED constant defined twice in the same file
description: `const HNSW_SEED: u64 = 42;` is copy-pasted verbatim inside both `build_from_db` (line 97) and `from_snapshot` (line 180). If the seed ever changes, both sites must be updated in sync. Current state: two local `const` items with identical values at different lexical scopes. Target state: one module-level `const HNSW_SEED: u64 = 42;` referenced by both functions. Refactoring pattern: Extract Constant. Motivation: DRY / divergence risk. Estimated scope: 1 file, 2 lines changed. Prerequisites: none. Risk: zero — purely mechanical.

title: SearchMode and MatchType lack Copy despite being pure-value enums
description: Both `SearchMode` (3 unit variants) and `MatchType` (5 unit variants) contain no heap-allocated data, yet neither derives `Copy`. Engine code calls `mode.clone()` in `infer_search_mode` (engine/query.rs:172), and match arms must take by reference where a copy would be cleaner. Current state: `#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]` and `#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, serde::Serialize, serde::Deserialize)]`. Target state: add `Copy` to both derives. Refactoring pattern: Derive Copy. Motivation: ergonomics, removes implicit clone calls. Estimated scope: 2 lines in hybrid.rs, remove `.clone()` in engine/query.rs:172. Prerequisites: none. Risk: zero — `Copy` is a subset of `Clone`; no existing code breaks.

title: RRF k=60 is a magic number with no named constant or citation
description: `rrf_merge(&fts_pairs, &vec_pairs, 60)` at line 195 embeds the standard RRF smoothing constant without naming it. The function signature accepts any `u32`, but the only production call site always passes 60. Current state: unnamed literal. Target state: module-level `const RRF_K: u32 = 60;` with a doc comment referencing the Cormack & Clarke (2009) default. Refactoring pattern: Introduce Explaining Variable / Extract Constant. Motivation: readability, documents the empirical baseline. Estimated scope: 1 file, 2-line diff. Prerequisites: none. Risk: zero.

title: Silently lossy i64→usize cast via `n as usize`
description: `Ok(n as usize)` where `n: i64` is a raw cast that silently wraps on 32-bit targets and misinterprets negative counts on any target. SQLite `COUNT(*)` is always non-negative, but the type system does not prove this. Clippy `cast_possible_truncation` / `cast_sign_loss` would flag this. Current state: `Ok(n as usize)`. Target state: `Ok(usize::try_from(n).unwrap_or(0))` — explicit handling of the (impossible in practice) negative or overflow case. Refactoring pattern: Replace Implicit Cast with Explicit Conversion. Motivation: correctness on 32-bit targets, clippy compliance. Estimated scope: 1 line. Prerequisites: none. Risk: negligible.
suggested_fix:
// fts.rs:119
Ok(usize::try_from(n).unwrap_or(0))

title: row_to_activity uses positional column indices (row.get(0..12)) instead of named access
description: Current state: row_to_activity (lines 209-236) uses `row.get(0)`, `row.get(1)`, ..., `row.get(12)` throughout. Every other row-mapping function in the module (and across the codebase) uses `row.get("column_name")`. Positional access breaks silently when the SELECT column order changes. Target state: replace all positional indices with named access, consistent with the rest of the codebase. Refactoring pattern: Replace Magic Number with Named Constant / Named Access. Motivation: fragility — a reordered SELECT silently produces wrong field assignments. Estimated scope: activities.rs only (single function). Risk: minimal.

title: LIMIT embedded via format!() in SQL string instead of bound parameter in two methods
description: Current state: `list_active` (facts.rs:132-147) and `list_by_session` (activities.rs:121-138) use `format!("... LIMIT {n}")` to embed the limit directly in the SQL string. All other methods that accept a limit use `params![limit as i64]` with a `?N` placeholder (e.g. `list_recent` in checkpoints.rs:88). SQLite supports LIMIT as a bound parameter. Inconsistency requires readers to trust the integer interpolation is safe. Target state: bind LIMIT as a parameter universally. Refactoring pattern: Parameterize. Motivation: consistency; reduces the cognitive burden of auditing format! SQL interpolations. Estimated scope: 2 methods across 2 files. Risk: minimal.

title: bool-to-i64 cast uses pinned as i64 in one place and i64::from(fact.is_pinned) in another
description: Current state: `set_pinned` at line 506 uses `rusqlite::params![pinned as i64, id]`. The `insert` method at line 94 uses `i64::from(fact.is_pinned)`. Both produce the same result but `as` casting is discouraged by clippy pedantic (cast_lossless), while `i64::from(bool)` is the idiomatic lossless conversion. Target state: uniform use of `i64::from(pinned)` at line 506. Refactoring pattern: Harmonize. Motivation: style consistency, clippy compliance. Estimated scope: 1 line in facts.rs. Risk: zero.

title: Date arithmetic assertion allows day 29 as a defensive hedge but the hedge is unnecessary and masks a real precision concern
description: The test archive_policy_default_has_30_day_cutoff (types.rs:76-83) asserts diff.num_days() == 30 || diff.num_days() == 29. The calculation is diff = Utc::now() - (Utc::now() - Duration::days(30)), which is always exactly 30 days unless clock drift between the two Utc::now() calls crosses a midnight boundary — an extremely unlikely event and not a real risk. The || 29 arm was written defensively but it masks a real future regression: if the default is accidentally changed to 29 days, the test still passes. This is a weak assertion pattern.
suggested_fix:
Replace:
```rust
assert!(diff.num_days() == 30 || diff.num_days() == 29);
```
With:
```rust
assert_eq!(diff.num_days(), 30);
```
If sub-second clock jitter is a concern, use Duration::seconds(30 * 86400) in the comparison instead of num_days.

title: mod.rs has no inline tests — re-exports are not smoke-tested
description: src/archive/mod.rs (11 lines) re-exports ArchiveManifestEntry, ArchivePolicy, ArchiveStats, and ArchiveVerifyResult but has no test block. While the re-exports are indirect coverage via integration tests, a module-level compile check that all four public types are constructible would catch accidental field renaming at the module boundary. This is a minor quality gap.
suggested_fix: A single compile-only doc-test on each re-exported type, or a trivial #[test] fn public_types_are_usable() that constructs a default ArchivePolicy and destructures ArchiveStats, would provide compile-time coverage of the re-export surface.

title: No public item in the archive module has a runnable /// # Example doc-test
description: All public functions and types in src/archive/ (write_pak, write_pak_and_hash, read_pak, hash_file, verify_pak in pak.rs; search_archives in search.rs; ArchivePak, ArchivePolicy, ArchiveStats, ArchiveManifestEntry, ArchiveVerifyResult in types.rs) have doc-comments but no ```rust example blocks. The absence means cargo test --doc exercises nothing in this module. Given that write_pak + read_pak is the core round-trip, a short ```no_run or ```ignore example on write_pak_and_hash and read_pak would both document usage and serve as a compile check.

title: Early-exit for missing session_id only tested with totally empty input
description: The no-session_id early exit (mod.rs:64-67) returns without error when JSONL is parseable but no entry carries a `sessionId` field. The only integration test covering the early path (`bootstrap_empty_file`) uses a completely empty reader — which triggers the same branch via `entries` being empty but tests a different code shape. A JSONL file with valid entries but no `sessionId` is not tested.

title: Property-based test missing for `BootstrapReport::merge` weighted-average invariant
description: `merge` recomputes `avg_importance` as a weighted average of two sub-populations (lines 65-69). The one existing `report_merge` test uses hand-chosen constants. The invariant `a.merge(&default()) == a` (identity merge) and the weighted-average monotonicity are not checked by property tests. The `proptest` crate is already in the workspace.

title: pytest and `[master` heuristic branches in outcome detection are untested
description: `detect_tests_passed` contains a pytest-specific branch (`lower.contains("pytest") && (... "passed" || " ok")`) at line 155 that no test exercises. Similarly, `detect_commit` checks `lower.contains("[master")` at line 118 but the only tested pattern is `[main`. These lines will not regress a naive refactor, but they also provide no documented contract for what inputs are accepted.

title: Strong property-based testing candidates lack both example-based and property tests
description: Two functions are particularly strong proptest candidates and currently have zero tests of any kind: (1) truncate_str: the property 'result.chars().count() <= max_chars' and 'result ends with ... iff input was truncated' are straightforward to express and cover the Unicode + boundary space automatically. (2) validate_jsonl_fact: the property 'importance in [0,1] && t_valid < t_invalid => Ok, else Err' is clean and would catch boundary issues (e.g., importance=0.0 and importance=1.0 must be Ok, t_valid==t_invalid must Err). No proptest or quickcheck dependency is present.

title: PassthroughEmbedder::embed_batch error path for 0 texts is untested
description: embed_batch returns Err for texts.len() != 1. This is tested for the case of >1 texts only incidentally if add_facts_batch calls it with multiple texts; neither case (0 texts, >1 texts) has a direct unit test. The embed_batch trait method has a default impl in most contexts so this method might rarely be called, but the error message mentions '0 texts' as a potential caller which would be confusing (the message says 'cannot batch-embed N texts' for N=0 too).

title: Public functions with behavioral doc comments lack runnable doc-test examples
description: truncate_str (output.rs:15) has a two-line doc comment making behavioral claims ('Safe for multi-byte UTF-8 — never slices mid-character') but no /// Example block. open_engine and open_engine_writable (db.rs:32-55) have detailed doc comments explaining read-only vs. write semantics but no examples. Missing doc-tests means the documented claims are not mechanically verified by cargo test --doc.

title: Already-expired fact re-resolution (double Update/Delete) is untested
description: The SQL at temporal.rs:179 includes `WHERE id = ?2 AND t_expired IS NULL`. This means calling `resolve_conflict` with Update or Delete on a fact that was already expired returns `MemoryError::NotFound`. This is a meaningful contract — callers that race or retry would receive this error — but no test exercises it. Adding a test also validates the `AND t_expired IS NULL` guard hasn't been accidentally removed.

title: pub fn resolve_conflict has no doc-test example
description: `pub fn resolve_conflict` is the only public item re-exported from `src/conflict/mod.rs:5` and documented with a full behavioural comment (temporal.rs:18-34). There are zero ```` ```rust ```` fences in either conflict source file. Other modules in this workspace (search/hybrid.rs, scope/tree.rs) carry runnable doc-test examples. A minimal doc-test would serve as live executable documentation and catch API signature drift at `cargo test --doc`.

title: FixedArbiter mock duplicated between inline test and eval helpers
description: `FixedArbiter` is defined identically in `src/conflict/temporal.rs:217-226` (inline test mock) and `tests/eval/helpers.rs:77-85` (integration eval mock). `helpers.rs:3` explicitly disclaims deduplication: `// Self-contained — does NOT deduplicate helpers in other test files`. As the module grows or the `ConflictArbiter` trait signature evolves, both definitions must be updated in sync. A drift (e.g. one not updated after a new trait method) would give silently diverging test behavior. This is an intentional choice per the comment, but worth flagging as a maintenance hazard.
suggested_fix: Either accept the duplication (it is intentional per the helpers.rs comment) and annotate both definitions with `// NOTE: also defined in tests/eval/helpers.rs`, or extract a `pub(crate)` `FixedArbiter` in a `#[cfg(test)]` helper in lib.rs / a dedicated `src/test_utils.rs` module, shared by both.

title: Dedup tie-break rule (importance comparison → expiry decision) suited for property-based testing
description: The expiry decision at dedup.rs:78-85 is a pure, stateless priority function: 'expire lower importance; on equal importance expire higher id'. This has testable invariants — exactly one of the pair is chosen, the survivor is always the one with higher importance (or lower id on tie), the expired id matches the actual DB state — that proptest can check across arbitrary `(importance_a, importance_b, id_a, id_b)` tuples without any DB interaction. Currently only 3 example cases are tested: `higher_importance_survives`, `equal_importance_newer_expires`, and `survivor_inherits_max_importance`.
suggested_fix: Extract the expiry decision into a small pure helper function (e.g., `fn choose_survivor(a_id: i64, a_imp: f64, b_id: i64, b_imp: f64) -> i64`) and add a proptest that generates arbitrary pairs, calls it, and asserts: (1) result is always one of the two ids; (2) if importances differ, the higher-importance id survives; (3) if importances are equal, the lower id survives.

title: only_compares_new_facts_against_active uses Utc::now() for both fixture timestamp and since filter, creating a potential flaky race
description: The test `only_compares_new_facts_against_active` (dedup.rs:192) derives `old_time = Utc::now() - Duration::days(10)` and then inserts a 'new' fact with `t_created: Utc::now()` (dedup.rs:225). The `since` filter is `old_time + Duration::days(1)`. The problem: the 'new' fact is classified as 'new' only if `t_created > since`. Since both `old_time` and the 'new' fact's `t_created` come from independent `Utc::now()` calls that may differ by microseconds, there is a vanishingly small but non-zero probability the new fact's `t_created` is slightly before `since` (e.g., if the clock is adjusted between calls). More practically, both `t_created: Utc::now()` calls inside the test helper (dedup.rs:145,153) and the insert_fact helper (dedup.rs:145) use live wall clock time, making the test sensitive to sub-millisecond ordering.
suggested_fix: Fix the `t_created` of the 'new' fact to an explicit future time relative to `since`: e.g., `t_created: since + Duration::seconds(1)`. This makes the test deterministic without wall-clock sensitivity. The existing `insert_fact` helper does not accept `t_created`; either add a `t_created` parameter or use the manual `store.insert(&NewFact{...})` form already present in that test for the 'old' fact.

title: source_fact_ids ordering assertion in global_integration test relies on DB insertion order
description: The test `global_integration_summarizes_clusters` (global.rs:109) asserts `global[0].source_fact_ids == vec![0, 1, 2]` (line 137). The `all_source_ids` vector is built in global.rs:63-66 by iterating `cluster_summaries` in `list_by_level` return order, then flat-mapping each summary's `source_fact_ids`. The assertion implicitly requires: (1) `list_by_level` returns summaries in insertion order; (2) each summary's `source_fact_ids` is stored and retrieved in insertion order. Both are SQLite-order-dependent implementation details. If the store changes to sort by a different column, this test fails with no real bug.
suggested_fix: Replace the strict equality with an order-independent assertion: `assert_eq!(global[0].source_fact_ids.iter().copied().collect::<std::collections::HashSet<_>>(), [0i64, 1, 2].iter().copied().collect::<std::collections::HashSet<_>>())`. Alternatively, sort both sides before comparing: `let mut ids = global[0].source_fact_ids.clone(); ids.sort(); assert_eq!(ids, vec![0, 1, 2]);`

title: local_dedup with zero active facts (empty DB) has no unit test
description: `local_dedup` on an empty DB (zero active facts) takes the fast path through the `new_facts` loop with no iterations. The function returns `Ok((0, vec![]))`, which is correct, but this edge case is never explicitly tested. The function does call `fact_store.list_active(None)?` which should succeed on an empty DB, but this is not verified. This matters because `list_active` could theoretically return an error or behave unexpectedly if the schema is partially initialized.
suggested_fix: Add a test `empty_db_dedup_is_noop` that calls `local_dedup(&conn, dim, 0.90, None, Utc::now())` on a freshly initialized DB with no facts, and asserts the result is `Ok((0, vec![]))`.

title: Only doc-test in scope is marked rust,ignore — zero runnable examples across public API
description: The only ```` ```rust ```` block across the five in-scope files is in `AsyncMemoryEngine`'s struct doc at async_engine.rs:28, and it is annotated `rust,ignore` — it does not execute during `cargo test --doc`. All other public items (`EmbeddingProvider`, `ForgetPolicy`, `DreamCycle`, `DreamCycleConfig::validate`, `MemoryError`, `Fact`, `ScopeQuery`, `PromoteRequest`) have no runnable doc-examples at all. CONTRIBUTING.md (project root) explicitly requires rustdoc examples for new public API items.

title: Four Display impls in types.rs have no test
description: `Outcome::fmt` (line 33), `FactType::fmt` (line 59), `ConsolidationLevel::fmt` (line 77), and `ActivityStatus::fmt` (line 437) are all public `Display` impls with no coverage in the inline test module. While these are low-complexity match arms, any case added to the enum without updating `fmt` would silently reach unreachable code or panic in debug builds; a test locks down the expected string values. `ActivityStatus` is the highest priority because it pairs with `FromStr` (see separate finding) and both string values must agree.

title: lib.rs has no #[cfg(test)] module; re-exports are not smoke-tested
description: lib.rs (62 lines) has no inline test module. Its role is to wire re-exports (lines 47-62). While individual modules have their own tests, the re-export surface — including `pub use error::*`, `pub use types::*`, `pub use traits::{DreamCycle, EmbeddingProvider, InsightStream, Reranker}`, and the Phase 5a `pub use engine::cognitive::DreamContext` at line 61 — is not exercised from lib.rs itself. A compilation smoke-test would catch a re-export accidentally shadowed or removed. The risk is low but the fix is trivial.

title: embed_batch() empty-input short-circuit has no test
description: embed_batch returns Ok(Vec::new()) immediately when texts.is_empty() (lines 184-186) without making an HTTP request. This is a meaningful edge case — callers should be able to rely on the guarantee that zero inputs produce zero outputs with no network I/O. No inline test or integration test covers this path.

title: No runnable doc-examples on the public API; lib.rs has no crate-level doc
description: HttpEmbeddingProvider (line 10) and its constructor new() (line 22) have no /// # Examples blocks. lib.rs (3 lines) has no //! crate-level documentation. Without runnable examples, cargo test --doc finds nothing to run for this crate, meaning compilation-breaking API changes in the doc-example layer go undetected. The # Errors section on new() (lines 19-21) is correctly present, but a basic constructing example would both document usage and serve as a compile-time regression guard.

title: Bearer auth is only tested for embed(), not for embed_batch()
description: The integration test bearer_auth_sent_when_configured (memory-engine-mcp/tests/embedding_integration.rs:267) exercises the Authorization header path in embed() (http.rs:122-124). The parallel code path in embed_batch() (http.rs:193-195) — identical logic, separate branch — has no corresponding test. If the bearer_auth call were accidentally removed from the batch path, no test would catch it.
suggested_fix: Add a test to the embed crate integration suite (once created per embed/testing-public-api-untested-in-crate) that mounts a wiremock mock requiring the Authorization header and calls embed_batch() with one or more texts, asserting the call succeeds (i.e. the auth header is actually sent).

title: Forward-compat `_ => {}` branch in `get_outcome_counts` is never exercised
description: At `outcome.rs:94`, the match arm `_ => {}` silently skips outcome strings that don't match `"Positive"`, `"Negative"`, or `"Neutral"`. This is intentional forward-compatibility behavior, but no test inserts a row with an unknown outcome string and asserts the resulting `OutcomeCounts` counts are unaffected. Without this test, a future schema migration that renames an outcome variant would silently produce zero counts instead of a visible error.
suggested_fix: In the inline `#[cfg(test)]` block of `outcome.rs` (or a new integration test), insert a raw row into the `fact_outcomes` table with `outcome_class = 'Future'`, then call `get_outcome_counts(fact_id)` and assert `counts.positive == 0 && counts.negative == 0 && counts.neutral == 0`. This documents the intended silent-skip behavior as an explicit contract.

location: src/engine/mod.rs (pub fn open, open_memory, add_fact, query, consolidate, forget)
title: Major public API methods have no runnable `# Examples` doc-tests
description: The six primary public methods — `open`, `open_memory`, `add_fact`, `query`, `consolidate`, and `forget` — all have prose documentation but zero runnable `# Examples` blocks. `cargo test --doc` produces no doc-test cases for the core API. This means documentation examples are never compile-checked, and new consumers have no self-contained runnable snippets illustrating the intended usage pattern (especially the trait-injection pattern required to call `add_fact` and `query`).

title: compute_importance output bounds never asserted
description: `compute_importance` is documented to compute a weighted sum of 4 signals each normalized to [0, 1]. Per ADR-0006 (weights intentionally need not sum to 1.0), the result is compared against `min_importance`, not against 1.0. However, no test asserts that the return value is non-negative for any valid input combination. In the existing tests the return value is only compared relationally (A > B), never checked for sign or finiteness. If a caller ever passes a `fact.importance` value outside [0, 1] (which is not validated by `ForgetPolicy::validate`), the composite score could become negative, causing facts to always be pruned regardless of threshold.
suggested_fix: Add a proptest that generates arbitrary valid `ForgetPolicy` instances and arbitrary `graph_degree` / `fact.access_count` / `fact.importance` values in [0, 1] and asserts `compute_importance(...) >= 0.0 && compute_importance(...).is_finite()`. Also add an example-based test at the boundary: `access_count = u32::MAX` (cast to f64 → saturates frequency to 1.0) and `graph_degree = usize::MAX` (caps connectivity to 1.0).

title: Negative age clamping (.max(0.0)) path is untested
description: Line 50 computes `age_days.max(0.0)` to guard against a `last_accessed` timestamp in the future (e.g., a fact added with `last_accessed = Utc::now() + Duration::hours(1)` via `AddFactOptions`). This clamp silently treats future-dated facts as age=0 (maximum recency). The clamping path is never exercised by any test — no test constructs a fact whose `last_accessed` is strictly after `now`. The silent-discard behavior (age becomes 0, recency becomes 1.0) is unspecified in comments and could surprise callers.

title: Integration eval tests rely on wall-clock time with non-injectable now
description: All four tests in `tests/eval/quality/forgetting.rs` construct facts with `days_ago(N)` timestamps (calling `Utc::now()` at fact-insertion time) and then call `engine.forget(&policy)`, which internally calls `Utc::now()` again at prune time (see `src/engine/forgetting.rs:27`). The computed importance scores rely on the age being exactly N days; if there is any wall-clock skew between the two `Utc::now()` calls (e.g. system clock adjustment, leap-second, NTP sync during CI), the scores could shift. The margins are large enough (45-365 days) that this is not a practical concern, but the root cause is architectural: `engine.forget()` does not accept an injectable `now: DateTime<Utc>` parameter, making it impossible to write deterministic time-travel tests. This is a latent design constraint that will limit testability for Phase 5 (DreamCycle scheduling).
suggested_fix: Consider adding an internal `forget_at(policy, now: DateTime<Utc>)` entry-point (or a test-only helper on `MemoryEngine`) that forwards a fixed `now` directly to `crate::forgetting::prune(...)`. This would allow eval tests to pin time exactly and eliminate the two-Utc::now() gap. The public `forget(&policy)` API stays unchanged and calls `forget_at(policy, Utc::now())` internally.

title: MCP handle_forget does not test invalid half_life_overrides key or non-object type
description: The `handle_forget` function in the MCP layer parses `half_life_overrides` as a JSON object (lines 1007-1030) and calls `parse_fact_type(key)` for each key. If the JSON contains an unrecognized fact-type string (e.g. `{"Unknown": 30.0}`) or if `half_life_overrides` is passed as a JSON array (`[30.0]`) rather than an object, it should return a `ValidationError`. The MCP test `test_forget_with_overrides` (tools.rs:163) only exercises the happy path with a valid `{"Episodic": 30.0}` override. Neither the invalid-key error path nor the non-object type error path (the `_ =>` arm at line 1023) is covered by any test.

title: load_from_db test covers only 1 active + 1 expired edge; empty table, weight preservation, and parallel edges are untested
description: The single load_from_db_skips_expired test uses weight: 1.0 for both edges and never asserts that weight (or relation_type) is correctly loaded into EdgeData. It also does not test the empty-table case (graph.node_count() == 0), self-loops (source == target), or parallel edges (same source/target pair, different edge_id). Petgraph DiGraph allows parallel edges; the load path at line 196-205 will insert all of them, but no test verifies that edge_count is correct in that scenario.
suggested_fix:
Extend the test suite with:
1. An empty-DB load: `assert_eq!(MemoryGraph::load_from_db(&conn).unwrap().edge_count(), 0)`
2. A weight-preservation check: insert with `weight: 0.42` and assert `snap.edges[0].weight == 0.42` after `to_snapshot()`
3. A parallel-edges load: two edges with same source/target but different relation_types, assert `edge_count == 2`

title: Strong property-based test candidates exist for graph invariants but proptest is unused in the graph module
description: proptest is already a dev-dependency (Cargo.toml:41) and is used in src/search/hybrid.rs, src/search/vector.rs, src/scope/tree.rs, and src/store/facts.rs. The graph module has several invariants that are excellent candidates for automated property testing but currently have only example-based tests: (1) degree(x) == outgoing(x) + incoming(x) for any topology; (2) connected_component(x) always contains x; (3) for any edge added then removed by edge_id, edge_count returns to its prior value; (4) from_snapshot(to_snapshot(g)) preserves edge_count and per-node degree.
references: src/search/hybrid.rs:491 (proptest pattern already used in codebase)

title: EdgeStats and ScopeStats only tested at zero baseline
description: `EdgeStats.active`, `.expired` and `ScopeStats.max_depth` are always 0 in all test scenarios (no edges are ever created, no sub-scopes are added). Similarly, `FactStats.expired` is always 0. The SQL queries for these fields are exercised but their non-zero return paths are never verified, making future SQL regressions invisible.
suggested_fix: Add a test with sub-scopes: call `add_fact` with a scoped path like `"project/module"`, then assert `stats.scopes.max_depth >= 1`. Add a test with expired facts (set `t_expired` via raw SQL) and assert `stats.facts.expired == 1`. Add edges via consolidation and assert `stats.edges.active >= 1`.

title: HashMap in EngineSnapshot.config and SummaryStats.by_level produces non-deterministic serialization
description: `EngineSnapshot.config` (types.rs:164) is `HashMap<String, String>` and `SummaryStats.by_level` (types.rs:204) is `HashMap<ConsolidationLevel, i64>`. `stream_snapshot` serializes `config` via `serde_json::to_writer` (dump.rs:71) without sorting. Two dumps of the same database produce different byte streams if HashMap iteration order differs (which Rust's `HashMap` does not guarantee). The insta snapshot tests paper over this by using `insta::sorted_redaction()` on config, but the serialized file itself is not deterministic — byte-level diff tools, checksums, or external consumers comparing snapshots will see spurious differences.
suggested_fix: Change `EngineSnapshot.config` from `HashMap<String, String>` to `BTreeMap<String, String>` (alphabetic key order, deterministic serialization). Similarly change `SummaryStats.by_level` to `BTreeMap<ConsolidationLevel, i64>` (requires `Ord` on `ConsolidationLevel`). This is mechanical — `BTreeMap` implements the same `Serialize`/`Deserialize` interface.

location: src/inspect/dump.rs:236, src/inspect/explain.rs:204, src/inspect/restore.rs:427, src/inspect/statistics.rs:134, tests/inspect_test.rs:15, tests/restore_roundtrip_test.rs:10
title: FakeEmbed/TestEmbed embedding stub duplicated six times across inspect tests
description: An identical 3-line `EmbeddingProvider` stub returning `vec![0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4]` (or `vec![0.25; DIM]`) is independently defined as `FakeEmbed` or `TestEmbed` in each of the four inline test modules and both integration test files. Any change to the trait signature or the 4-dimensional convention requires updating six copies. This is a maintenance hazard and obscures intent.
suggested_fix: Extract a single `FakeEmbed` (or `ConstEmbed`) into `src/inspect/test_utils.rs` (or `tests/common.rs` for integration tests) gated with `#[cfg(test)]`, and `use super::test_utils::FakeEmbed` in each module. Alternatively, add a `testing` feature flag and expose a `memory_engine::testing::FakeEmbed` re-export.

title: All public inspect functions have prose doc-comments but no runnable doc-tests
description: Every public function in the inspect module (`dump_json`, `dump_json_gzip`, `dump_json_zstd`, `dump_sqlite`, `explain_fact`, `fact_history`, `read_snapshot`, `validate_snapshot`, `restore_snapshot_into`, `compute_statistics`, `to_event_filter`) has `/// Error` documentation but no ` ```rust ` example block. Consumers of the library have no in-doc demonstration of correct usage, and doc-tests that run under `cargo test --doc` are absent entirely for this module. The insta snapshot tests have the same gap — they verify structure but not usage patterns.
suggested_fix: Add minimal runnable examples to at least the three most-used entry points: `explain_fact`, `read_snapshot`, and `compute_statistics`. Each example should use `MemoryEngine::open_memory`, add a fact, call the function, and assert an obvious property. Mark examples `no_run` only if they truly require filesystem state that cannot be created in a doc-test context.

title: TestEmbedder, args(), and unwrap_ok() helpers are duplicated across four test files
description: The blake3-based TestEmbedder struct is defined verbatim in tests/tool_roundtrip.rs (line 19-41), tests/depth_shaping.rs (line 15-36), and tests/query_mode_inference.rs (line 19-41). The args() helper (Map-from-Value) and unwrap_ok() (extract JSON from CallToolResult) are duplicated across all five test files. Duplication means any change to the TestEmbedder normalisation algorithm (e.g. to switch to a different hash function) must be applied in three places and can drift silently.
suggested_fix: Create tests/common/mod.rs containing the canonical TestEmbedder, args(), and unwrap_ok() definitions. In each test file, replace the local definitions with `mod common; use common::*;` (or `#[path = "common/mod.rs"] mod common;` if test file layout is flat). This is a mechanical refactor that requires no judgement about test semantics.

title: open() with read_pool_size=0 on a file-backed path is untested and silently routes reads through write_conn
description: ConnectionPool::open(path, embed_dim, 0, None) is a valid call (read_pool_size: usize, no validation). It stores read_pool_size=0 and path=Some(path). When read() is subsequently called, line 188 checks `if self.read_pool_size == 0` and takes the InMemory branch, locking write_conn for reads — the same serialized path as an in-memory database. This is semantically surprising for a file-backed pool: there is no Condvar notification path, query_only is never set on the write connection for this case, and the pool appears file-backed (is_file_backed() returns true) while behaving like in-memory. No test exercises this edge case; EngineConfig defaults to 4, but the public API permits 0.

title: path() accessor has no unit test
description: ConnectionPool::path() (line 241) returns Option<&Path>. The existing tests verify is_file_backed() (line 311-319) but no test asserts that path() returns Some(db_path) for a file-backed pool or None for an in-memory pool. This is a trivial coverage gap for a public API method.

title: No proptest coverage for pool constructor parameter invariants
description: The codebase already uses proptest in several modules (src/search/hybrid.rs:503, src/store/facts.rs:1427, src/store/schema.rs:2070, etc.). ConnectionPool has numeric constructor parameters (embed_dim: usize, read_pool_size: usize) with implicit invariants: embed_dim stored and returned verbatim, read_pool_size == read_conns.len() after open(). These roundtrip invariants are strong proptest candidates — arbitrary embed_dim should always satisfy pool.embed_dim() == embed_dim, and read_pool_size should always satisfy pool.read() succeeding read_pool_size times without blocking (in-memory skipped). No proptest exists for the pool module.

title: No fuzz targets exist in the workspace for pool's untrusted-path inputs
description: There is no fuzz/ directory in the workspace. ConnectionPool::open_read_only() accepts a &Path from untrusted or user-supplied input (e.g., MCP tool arguments) and passes it through path.is_file() (file-system oracle) and then open_connection_read_only() which calls SQLite. Malformed or adversarial path strings (embedded NUL bytes, extremely long paths, symlinks to devices, paths pointing to non-SQLite files) are not exercised. The absence of a fuzz harness is a gap given the crate is an embedded library expected to handle arbitrary consumer-supplied paths.

title: Pool is never tested as an external consumer — all integration tests go through MemoryEngine
description: All files under tests/ (read_only_test.rs, roundtrip_test.rs, inspect_test.rs, etc.) use MemoryEngine as the entry point.
